item.title: The Birds Are Listening: Scientists Used Seabirds to Track Hidden Ships
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: In what sounds like an avian riff on , scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders in order to listen in on their interactions with fishing vessels across the world’s oceans, according to a study published on Wednesday in .The approach exposed a large number of so-called “unseen” vessels that did not have their location trackers switched on. Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship’s location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons—such as evading pirates—or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming “bycatch” when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.Unseen vessel activity “is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal,” said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a “powerful tool for improving risk assessment” by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map. Rutter and his colleagues were inspired to combine these approaches by attaching audio recorders to three seabird species—the northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel—which all frequently interact with fishing vessels. The team tracked the movements of the birds with GPS, and then analyzed whether the audio overlapped with AIS data at the same time and location during recorded interactions.The recordings showed that about 32 percent of the audio captured by seven gannets in the North Atlantic were from ships with their trackers off, while 12 percent of the audio captured by four shearwaters in the Mediterranean Sea were from unseen vessels. The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off.Rutter noted that the shearwaters were likely often interacting with smaller Mediterranean fishing boats that are not legally required to keep trackers on. However, the gannets encountered larger commercial vessels that are obligated to keep trackers active. While the researchers made a very conservative estimate that these birds visited unseen vessels for about one-third of the total duration of their daily encounters (or, about 22 minutes out of 68 minutes), it may well exceed half of that time.“The fact that we found at least one third, and probably more than one half, of the audio detections being unseen was pretty surprising,” Rutter said. “This is not the same thing as saying that half of vessels are unseen; it's half of the time that gannets go to vessels, those vessels are unseen.”“There are multiple reasons this could be,” he continued. “It could be illegal disabling, but at the same time, it could be poor satellite reception. There are lots of reasons that AIS can be off, and we want to emphasize that illegal fishing is a possibility, but that is not actually what we're showing. It's showing that there's a lot we're not seeing.”Seabirds are attracted to fishing vessels to feed on discarded catch, but many perish during these encounters after becoming tangled in lines or caught on baited hooks. Rutter and his colleagues hope that their study could help to prevent these deadly incidents, while also providing a new tool for monitoring unseen vessel activity. While this approach could enable real-time vessel detection, the team urged “caution in the use of animals as a fisheries surveillance tool, lest fishers come to mistrust scientists and/or marine animals themselves,” according to the study.Though environmental and commercial interests are often at odds, there is plenty of collaboration between fisheries and conservation scientists with the goal of sustainable and healthy long-term fish stock. Fisheries that adhere to regulations also have an interest in working with researchers to combat illegal activity by competitors.In addition, these audio recordings offer a new way to eavesdrop on wild seabird behavior. For example, the petrel’s recordings captured distinct landing and takeoff sequences previously observed in albatrosses, opening a new avenue of research into the flight patterns of this species. The recordings also highlight how human activity has upended food webs, as seabirds have become dependent on fishing vessel waste as a major source of food. “One of the advantages of this is that we can understand in a more unbiased way how much [seabirds] actually interact with vessels—every day, multiple times a day for all the species we looked at actually, which is crazy if you think about it,” Rutter said. “They're going out every day and just visiting boats all the time, and that shows the impact that we have on them as humans is really changing their feeding ecology,” he concluded.

item.content:encoded: As I write this morning, the day before Thanksgiving, Nvidia stock is trading at $141 per share. That means it’s given up roughly 3/4 of the value it gained after Monday’s shock announcement that Donald Trump had, paradoxically, midwifed Jensen Huang back into the CEO suite at Nvidia. I jokingly compared Huang’s return to Napoleon’s “100 Days” between his escape from exile on Elba to his final exile at St. Helena. Maybe I was being optimistic. Today I want to pull back to a broader view of this unfolding drama, which is the collision between the cultures of Silicon Valley and Washington, D.C., the swashbuckling world of Silicon Valley and national security state.

item.title: What are they hiding?
item.author: SRS0=motL=JO=bounces.e.demandjustice.org=bounces@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: Muneer, in January, Republicans lose control of the Senate. So they've decided to spend these last few weeks locking in Trump's crony judges for life. And they're moving so fast that they're skipping the basics:Nominees are getting hearings before the FBI has even finished their background checks. Chair Chuck Grassley is holding hearings week after week, packing in up to eight nominees at once. One Texas nominee was put up for a lifetime seat right after voters rejected him in his own state Supreme Court race. Another one's nomination was thrown together in a week. It started the day after the election, and he never went through the screening Texas nominees normally face.Why the rush? Because the closer you look at Trump's judges, the clearer it gets: these are We've seen it from the judges he's already put on the bench, more than 60 of them this term. They tell him what he wants to hear. They dodge the truth under oath, even about whether he lost in 2020. And they side with billionaires, big corporations, and Trump's extremist agenda over the people and the Constitution they swore to serve. Every nominee Republicans rush through now gets a lifetime seat. These judges will be ruling on our rights, our freedoms, and our economy long after Trump is gone. This is how you stack the courts. And we refuse to let it happen quietly. Demand Justice PAC is on the front lines of the fight to root out corruption from our courts. If Senate Republicans won't take a close look at these nominees, we will. We'll expose their records before the votes happen. And we'll make sure every senator who votes to confirm them owns that vote. Republicans are counting on speed to outrun scrutiny. We need the resources to keep up with every hearing and every vote between now and January.

item.title: This Thanksgiving, I Hope Someone Gets You Cookies
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season (except when there's a game on a Wednesday). Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over atIt’s the holiday season in Chicago, and I am six years old. My grandma Neenie is staying at her apartment in the Streeterville neighborhood of the city, just south of the John Hancock building. Neenie and Grandpa spend the bulk of the time living down in Palm Beach, Fla., but they’ve kept the Chicago apartment because this is where they raised my mother and her three siblings, and because my family lives there now, in an apartment farther uptown. I love it when Neenie and Grandpa visit, because I know that Neenie will take me to Water Tower Place and buy me shit.Water Tower Place is located just a few blocks away from my grandparents’ apartment, on the tony stretch of Michigan Avenue and right next to the old Chicago Avenue Pumping Station, after which the mall is named. You enter Water Tower Place from the ground floor, and then ride up into the mall alongside a series of little waterfalls cascading down between the twin escalators. I’m a grade-schooler, so I’m already predisposed to loving a good escalator ride. The fact that this one has waterfalls makes it, in my innocent mind, the most magical escalator in the world. Like riding up to heaven, if heaven had a McDonald’s in it.

item.title: I made a daily word game!
item.author: bounces+lmurrlxe4wcmh40rlxqc6h8843rv9igh75wl@ckespa.joshdoody.com
item.content:encoded: This is a short week and a holiday, so I'm doing something a little different for this week's newsletter: I'm telling you about Foreword, the free daily word game I made!It's inspired by Scattergories and Wordle and is a really quick, fun way to spend a couple minutes every day. You can play solo or in groups with friends and family.Each day, you get the day's letter (today's is "R") and 10 prompts like "Rainy day activities" or "Children's games" or "Magazines". You have two minutes to answer as many prompts as possible using words that start with the day's letter. You can even get multiple points for a single prompt if your answer has multiple words that start with the day's letter (like "Peppa Pig" for "Cartoon characters").Each game is graded by Fred, a pretty opinionated AI judge who can be a little snarky and appreciates creativity.I built Foreword because ... well because I wanted it to exist. I enjoy word games like Catch Phrase, Taboo, and Scattergories, and I play daily word games like Wordle, crosswords, and some NYT daily games. I thought, "Wouldn't it be fun to a daily word game that I can play with friends?" And I was off to the races.I've been playing every day for a few months, and there are about 70 people who play it each day now. Most people are in a group or two with friends and family, where they can see each other's answers and even react to them when they're funny (😂) or brilliant (💡) or suspect (🧐). Playing in groups is my favorite thing about Foreword, so start a group and invite some folks to join you!People have really been enjoying it, so I hope you'll check it out!Here's my result from today:Have a Happy Thanksgiving and enjoy the long weekend!PS Tomorrow is Thanksgiving and I've got some fun surprises in store. So make sure you play Foreword tomorrow!

item.title: A Less-Than-Satisfying End to a Landmark Trump II Legal Battle
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: I suspect many of you thought that Kilmar Abrego Garcia had prevailed in court long ago and may have been surprised to see him self-deport to Spain overnight. He reportedly hasn’t made a decision about his ultimate destination.But while the man subjected to a sustained campaign of brutalization by the Trump administrations had won landmark court cases, the law still gave the government enormous power over his ultimate fate — giving him few good choices.For many months now, Abrego Garcia had been trying to leave the country on his own, but the Trump administration had refused to allow it. It’s not clear what changed the equation for the administration, but by allowing him to leave now it does avoid having appeals courts weigh in on some of its most egregious conduct over the past two years.Let me briefly orient you, and then we’ll zoom back out to the big picture.There were essentially three Abrego Garcia cases, and he won all three:Wrongful deportation to El Salvador: Abrego Garcia was removed to CECOT in his home country the same March 2025 weekend as the Alien Enemies Act deportations in violation of an immigration judge’s order that barred his removal because of his fears of persecution and torture. He challenged his removal and took the case all the way to the Supreme Court, which, in a landmark ruling, ordered the Trump administration to “facilitate” his return.Vindictive criminal prosecution: Under order from the Supreme Court to facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return, the Trump DOJ indicted him on trumped-up human trafficking charges in Tennessee. When he returned to the United States, he was immediately put in federal custody on the criminal charges. He successfully challenged his prosecution as a vindictive response to his winning the civil case. The Trump DOJ’s appeal of that ruling was still pending, and just yesterday the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals scheduled oral arguments in the appeal for Feb. 24, 2027.: As its criminal case against Abrego Garcia was falling apart, the Trump administration began threatening to deport him to a series of African countries to which he had no ties even though Costa Rica came forward to say that it would take him. Abrego Garcia succeeded in winning release from custody after it became clear that the Trump administration was using the hollow threat of imminent third-country deportation to keep him detained. The Trump DOJ’s appeal of that ruling was still pending before the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals.Abrego Garcia’s expressed willingness to leave the country voluntarily had meant that for months there was an available exit ramp for the Trump administration if it chose to take it. Repeated delays agreed to by the parties in both of the pending appeals hinted that something might be in the works, but news of the arrangement only emerged last evening as Abrego Garcia was set to fly out of Dulles.With Abrego Garcia safely in Spain this morning, U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis of Maryland — who did yeoman’s work overseeing both the civil cases — issued an order dissolving the remaining injunctions, ruling on the remaining motions, and closing the case. The two pending appeals and the criminal case will presumably be closed now, too.Interestingly, Judge Xinis also unsealed a Nov. 20 order that now reveals what was in the works. The Nov. 20 order came after Judge Xinis engaged in a “consultation with the parties” on Oct. 6, an event that was not publicly listed on the court docket. Her subsequent order set the conditions of Abrego Garcia’s departure, including the departure date of Nov. 24. It also removed any remaining obstacles to his departure, including ordering his ankle monitor removed before he boarded the airplane, prohibiting the government from interfering with his departure or from treating it as a violation of any condition of his release.The Trump administration took one last parting shot at Abrego Garcia, re-upping its 20-month campaign of defaming and dehumanizing him:There remains one important bit of unfinished business. Judge Xinis still has a potential contempt of court inquiry pending into the conduct of the Trump DOJ and DHS from the first civil case. She had prioritized the substance of the legal challenges by Abrego Garcia but presumably can now return to that unresolved matter.While Abrego Garcia’s self-deportation may feel like an unsatisfactory conclusion to this saga, this has been the best plausible outcome for him for some time. It took extraordinary work from his legal teams in both the civil and criminal cases. It took bold and determined federal judges in Maryland and Tennessee. It took appeals courts having the backs of district judges.In the Trump II era, wins can be hard to come by, and they may not look as pretty and clear-cut as our pre-Trump selves would have wanted. But there’s a danger that we can redefine wins out of existence by setting the bar too high. This was a huge win for Abrego Garcia and his legal team while still being an abomination by the Trump administration.“For years, the Administration has treated the weaponization of law enforcement like a horror movie villain coming for them. Now the threat is finally real. Only the call is coming from inside the house—the White House. Perhaps, less time on the pool and more on reflecting.”—U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui of D.C., in a blistering opinion dismissing the politicized prosecution of veteran FBI agents Bradley Benavides and Nikki Cole FlorisThe Trump DOJ was forced to file an admission of error in federal court after it falsely described the legal position taken by the House general counsel on the FBI search of the D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN).“The United States apologizes for this inadvertent misunderstanding,” prosecutors from U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office said in the filing.Far from hanging Omar out to dry, the House’s top lawyer took a much more muted position than the Trump DOJ had previously conveyed to U.S. District Judge James Boasberg.The new filing includes a copy of the October email response from House general counsel Matthew Berry to Trent McCotter, who is now the acting deputy attorney general. In addition to revealong McCotter’s role in the error, it shows the vindictive investigation of Omar being directed by the highest levels of the Trump DOJ.Dems Win at Least 259 House SeatsThe AP finally called the TN-04 race for Democrat Victoria Broderick, who knocks off incumbent Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R), who had conceded days ago.In the Alaska Senate, incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) finally conceded to Democrat Mary Peltola.As a tribute to my late friend Paul Johnson, I am once again sharing his beloved turkey gumbo recipe. Friends don’t let friends waste a good roast turkey carcass.See you back here Monday.

item.title: San José State President Enlisted Harry Edwards To Sabotage Students’ Pro-Palestine Encampment
item.author: Samer Kalaf
item.content:encoded: As heartening as it was to see the wave of student-led Gaza solidarity encampments across college campuses in the spring of 2024, it was just as appalling to see the crackdowns from those same schools' administrations. Across the world, university leaders showed that they were willing to sacrifice the safety of their own students and faculty, rather than divest from any companies that had financial ties to a state committing active genocide.The most closely covered protest was at Columbia University, where the schoolultimately sent in the NYPD to dismantle the camp and assault students. The response dragged on for months; a WhatsApp group strategized on how to get the protestors deported, and put together a list of targets. Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil is currently appealing a deportation order, after he was held in ICE detention without criminal charges for over 100 days. On the other side of the country in 2024, UCLA's security and local police stood by as masked goons attacked students within the Gaza solidarity encampment, and tossed fireworks at them. Roughly 30 of the students and faculty attacked have sued UCLA for civil rights violations.Because of reporting last week from Bradford William Davis and Kaya Henkes-Power at the publication Eyeblack, another school administration's grimy efforts have come to light, two years later. When San José State University students put together their Gaza solidarity encampment in 2024, they convened at the statue, a monument on campus honoring the school's alumni Tommie Smith and John Carlos for their raised fists at the 1968 Summer Olympics. The statue was created in 2005 by the Portuguese artist Ricardo Gouveia, who goes by the moniker Rigo 23.

item.title: Hark! Royal Gossip Approaches!
item.author: Jae Towle Vieira
item.content:encoded: Have you ever wondered what a pack of specially trained bloodhounds might do for your personality? Ever considered the societal benefits of locking up your enemies in the Tower of London? Would a special dispensation from the Pope smooth things out for your most fraught marriage prospects? Could you deal with being hot enough to change the course of humanity? Prepare yourselves for the majesty of ! Rachelle Hampton and the team are back with a new miniseries that dares to ask the question: What is history if not gossip? Over the course of four episodes, we’ll explore the most sordid tales from one of the most charmed and chaotic periods in English history: The Wars of the Roses. Oh, and did we mention we’ll have royalty? In each episode of , Rachelle will be joined by our dowager queen Kelsey McKinney!

item.title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Is A Thrilling Homecoming For James Gray
item.author: Robert Rubsam
item.content:encoded: Americans are forever returning to their origins, because we are always beginning again. At the start of the 20th century, three-fourths of my ancestors were still in Europe; my mother’s parents did not come over until the end of the second World War. To think of all the accidents and contingencies that brought me here, to this laptop in this café writing about the latest film by James Gray, is enough to trigger vertigo in anyone. Where does my story start? With my birth, or when my parents met on an airplane, or when my dad’s grandparents met as new immigrants in Queens? Is it only beginning now, as I type these words? Has it even begun yet?I think Gray might understand. A director of New York City crime sagas and classically toned period pieces, his films probe the intimate in search of the mythic, and frequently achieve a kind of outer-borough biblicality. , his latest and quite possibly his best, is a story of shifting loyalties inside a Queens family called the Pearls. Irwin (Miles Teller) is an engineer, a “facts and figures” guy with a moderately successful small business, a house in Fresh Meadows, and a sea of expenses rising all around him. His wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) wants to move to suburban Great Neck; his sons need tuition for private school and the Ivy League stamp that Irwin believes will vault them out of the ethnic middle class, and allow them to achieve what their Pratt-educated father never could. Over Labor Day weekend of 1986, the Pearls are visited by Irwin’s brother, Gary (Adam Driver), a recently divorced ex-cop with shiny suits, a sports car, and seemingly liquid cash flow. Swooping into their two-story brick home with a steak meal hand-delivered from Peter Luger, he wants to cut Irwin in on a lucrative opportunity, joining their security and engineering knowledge to consult on the clean-up of the outlandishly polluted Gowanus Canal. New York is changing, the Italian mob is in decline, and the canal’s new landowners are all Russian Jews like the Pearls, though of more recent vintage. “Communism’s over,” Gary explains. “Everyone wants their piece of the pie.”

item.title: Thanksgiving dinner, brought to you by K Street
item.author: SRS0=etN6=JO=amazonses.com=010001a21370e440-a5db759f-5f81-43d0-8110-c9a66502acf5-000000@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: With Senate Democrats preparing to choose their next leader, the two contenders for the job took notably different approaches with their leadership PAC and joint fundraising committee money, . Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s leadership PAC distributed a net $252,500 to candidates and party committees during the cycle, according to an OpenSecrets analysis of Federal Election Commission filings. By comparison, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland directed $262,000 to fellow candidates and party committees through his leadership political action committee and helped four battleground Senate candidates raise more than $421,000 through joint fundraising committees. The contrast offers a window into their different approaches to political giving ahead of the Dec. 1 vote for majority leader, after Democrats won control of the chamber. Van Hollen wrote more checks directly to candidates and supplemented them with joint fundraising committees, while Schumer’s leadership PAC gave a larger share of its money to party committees.

item.title: A ‘Distraction’ Reunion On ‘All Ball’, Just For You
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: The NFL’s Thanksgiving weekend slate starts tonight, with the wholly manufactured “Thanksgiving Eve” game on Netflix. This slate features a ton of juicy matchups, almost as recompense for the previous two weeks of dreadful games that you and I have had to endure. Every one of the five-throwgasm showdowns spread out across the next six days(!) merits thorough analysis. Alas, because my co-host Arif Hasan was on the road all day yesterday, you the audience get David Roth instead. https://art19.com/shows/the-distraction/episodes/000e8d43-8c45-4d22-b035-1f0e5cbf58fe My old co-host is versed in football, so don’t be alarmed. You’ll still get plenty of chitchat about the games at hand. But Roth and I also carve out some time to marvel at the election results, to ask big-picture questions about the league’s desire to occupy every available time slot, and to discuss Portuguese egg tarts. Truly, a feast for the ears. As always, we do NOT talk about gambling or fantasy football. Roth tried to get in a brief fantasy note, but I quickly shut that talk down and had my friend summarily killed after we’d recorded this episode. Didn’t want to do it; felt I it to him.

item.title: This stupid shit can’t even pardon a turkey without being an asshole about it
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: We all know that Little Donny Fuckface is a quadrice-indicted twice-impeached once-convicted popular-vote-losing adderall-huffing dead-pedo-bestie-schmoozing East-Wing-destroying insurrection-leading ear-diapering testimony-ducking judge-threatening lawyer-ignoring debate-avoiding witness-tampering crypto-scamming disabled-veteran-dishonoring insider-trading inheritance-squandering rube-fleecing clown-makeup-smearing language-mangling sneaker-hawking serial-sexual-predating draft-dodging casino-bankrupting butler-bullying daughter-perving hush-money-paying real-estate-swindling bone-spur-faking ketchup-hurling justice-obstructing classified-war-plan-thieving golf-cheating stock-manipulating weather-map-defacing war-criminal-pardoning horse-paste-promoting paper-towel-flinging race-baiting tax-evading evidence-destroying charity-defrauding money-laundering diaper-filling 34-count 80-year-old fluorescent-tangerine narcoleptic fart factory. But do you know what else Donny is? He’s a loathsome old shithead who compulsively craps all over everyone else’s good time.Let’s do that thing where I play a clip, and you try to guess what kind of event Donny was speaking at. Ready? . “The price of gasoline also has dropped twenty percent in the last— two weeks. You notice it dropped right after the election? So, uh— I wonder if somebody had that in mind. A little strange. That happened with the covid vaccine, right? Right after the election they announced we had a vaccine.”Okay — you’re never going to guess where Donny was, so let me just tell you. That was Preznit Fuckwit, pardoning this year’s White House turkeys.Now, the turkey pardoning is a thing that every president has done since forever. It’s supposed to be a light moment of fun that kicks off America’s long Thanksgiving holiday weekend.But Donny’s too fucking broken inside to ever have fun with . So instead of tossing off a cute little speech, he pisses and moans about every grudge and grievance. He gives the exact same whiny speech he always gives, in which he — the child of privilege who was born into obscene wealth, handed every opportunity, eternally bailed out and allowed to fail upwards forever, until he finally fell ass-backwards into the United States presidency, — is somehow always . Pity poor Donny, he always has it so rough. This tiresome fuckstick can’t even pardon a turkey without being an asshole about it. No one wants to hear that shit. Even the turkeys were like,It’s so exhausting. I’m tired of being ruled over by these tiny little defective homonculi who can never let the country experience even the briefest moment of pleasure. Everything has to be a . Even our country’s 250th birthday party turned out out to be joyless piece of shit, because these people have no idea how to I guess we should be thankful that at least Donny did manage to pardon the turkeys, after he was done whining. Acting President Stephen Miller would have probably just unhinged his jaw and swallowed them live.That was Obama, back in 2016. It’s a cute little event that lasts about a little over nine minutes.He’s got some super-adorable nephews with him, and he pretty much spends the whole time making corny dad jokes and telling awful puns. He’s having fun. The press is having fun. The guests are having fun. All of us watching right now, ten years later, are having fun.That’s how you do it. That’s how you pardon a fucking turkey.Oh, I’m sorry. Our current president, Shitticus J. Ratbrain, has more he wants to whine about. Let’s get back to him.“We created, the day before the election, we created twenty— did you know that, Mike? We created twenty-five— TRILLION dollars in wealth. We lost about six of it, because of the election. If we would have won the election, we would have probably gained another six. But the twenty-five trillion’s a record. No country’s done that in such a— short period of time.”I have a question. Where the fuck is this $25 trillion that ‘we’ created? Who’s we? If we’re all so rich, why did the Veterans Administration need to be gutted by the Space Nazi’s merry band of unfuckable DOGE incels? Why did USAID have to be shut down, if we’re rolling in that much dough?Why can’t schoolchildren get a simple free hot lunch?Donny, of course, is just making shit up. None of the numbers that just seeped out of his rancid anus-mouth are real. Why does Donny have to be a jerk about everything all the time? Do you imagine he was in a bad mood because he had to pardon those turkeys for ? But wouldn’t it be nice if we once again had a president who could just stand up and casually toss off a few bad puns, tell some corny jokes, pardon the damned turkeys and then leave us the fuck alone?“Based on your temperament and commitment to being productive members of society I hereby pardon Peach and Blossom.”Joe’s 2024 pardoning ceremony lasts just under nine minutes. He doesn’t tell as many silly jokes as Obama, but he’s clearly enjoying himself. He also gives his thanks and gratitude for having gotten to have a long political career. What do you imagine Donny is thankful for? I’m guessing it’s . He’s a greedy vulgarian who imagines he’s entitled to — and whatever he’s given, Imagine being that broken, that you’ve never known a minute of satisfaction.I’m thankful I’m not Donny.Oh and by the way, I keep hearing about how all during the last year of his presidency, Joe Biden was icky and old and smelled bad and was so demented that he didn’t even know he was already dead. I don’t know, he’s sounds pretty alert in this clip. Oh sure, he loses his train of thought a couple of times, but it’s nothing like our current cognitively-collapsed president, who can’t go six words without tripping over his own rhetorical dick. Why? What has Rudy Colludy done to merit this award?This photo so perfectly encapsulates why everything right now. Here we have two grinning idiots, standing in the now completely-defiled Oval Bordello, in font of a portrait of the fuckstain who enabled our country’s long decline into oligarchy.I’m thankful I’m not any of these shitweasels. Andrew Ross Sorkin: “The president does own shares of Nvidia. Do you genuinely think that President Trump, in the instances of doing things for companies … that relate to stock that he may own, do you believe that’s what’s driving him?”Jamie Raskin: “Well, if you don’t believe that, you're too innocent to be let out of the house by yourself.”Seriously. This has been today’s episode of Stupid Questions, Easy Answers. Hey, guess what: it’s time for our Daily Claudia.Today we have a trio of Katie and her mom at the Shipwright’s Daughter in Mystic, CT, on July 10, 2025.You’ve seen these three photos before, but I’m reposting them for a good reason.The Shipwright’s Daughter is one of our favorite restaurants in the world. Ms Spouse and I would dine there at least once, every time we were vacationing in the area. But they don’t just do excellent food — they do excellent. Right now, they’re helping to promote a benefit and fundraiser for the family of a local woman who was kidnapped by ICE and deported to Mexico, separating her from her husband and three children at home. Okay, enough of me droning on. Here’s the Daily Claudia.Have a great Wednesday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: A Royals Offseason Roadmap, Dictated by the Market
item.author: SRS0=Dv60=JO=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: A fitting baseball offseason colloquialism leading into Thanksgiving. As November dawns and World Series winners wrestle hangovers, the rest of the baseball world turns to the hot stove and, well, shopping lists. Digital ink is spilled on each club’s needs and how to best fulfill them, as if Major League Baseball, its clubs and free agents exist in a static roster-building simulation. Sign a starting pitcher. Check the box. Move on to the next priority. (Need two? The Boras Corp. Corner Store is offering a buy-one-get-one blowout sale!) But how roster construction really works — best I can tell, as someone prognosticating from a spare basement bedroom rather than pulling strings from a plush front office swivel chair — is less like a trip to the grocery store and more like a quest to buy the perfect used car. What starts as a need (lane assist, or a free agent left-handed starting pitcher) can quickly become a want — or out of reach entirely. Budgets are set beforehand but might be stretched for just the right fit. Maybe your scouts love a certain make/model but your manager (spouse? this metaphor is getting worse) prefers a sturdier build. Most importantly, the market drives everything. The car you dreamed of costs more than you expected, or it isn’t available in your area, or interest rates leap, or the rest of the league decides paying a premium for starting pitching is what’s required with a lockout looming. In all likelihood, the Royals envisioned themselves — maybe as recently as two weeks ago — largely filling out their rotation through free agency. It’s not a stretch to make that assumption. Seth Lugo and Michael Wacha are the prime examples.As negotiations opened earlier this month, my hunch is it became clear the organization would not be partaking in the sweepstakes for starters in the second tier of the market behind Tarik Skubal. Two candidates, left-hander Trevor Rogers and right-hander Freddy Peralta, each signed for five years this week; Rogers for $120 million, Peralta for $125 million. Many projections pegged each of the two for four-year agreements in the $75-100 million range, a far cry from the deals they’d eventually sign. And if my guess is correct, Kansas City realized its intention to splash cash at starting pitching would not provide the optimal route to contention. The market shifted. So did the Royals. Instead, they dealt third baseman Maikel Garcia — just one year into a long-term contract — as part of a package that included reliever James McArthur and minor league lefty LP Langevin for a haul of MLB-ready arms: RHP Bryce Miller, a high-upside starter; LHP Jose A. Ferrer, a ground-ball inducing bullpen weapon; and RHP Logan Evans, who profiles as a back-end starting pitcher and innings eater.I love GarciaShove+ gradesShove+ is my pitching model (limited to starting pitchers only, for now) that seeks to identify talent over production, using metrics like Stuff+, CSW% and Location+ to balance skill, control and ability to limit damage on contact.Based on 2026 evaluations, Miller will head into 2027 as the club’s most talented starter — by far.A lot of conclusions are being drawn that the club is operating from a desire to avoid spending money, instead choosing to deal from its cache of young, talented hitters to fill a rotation. Robbing Peter to pay Paul, in a sense. Those conclusions are being drawn in haste. It is Nov. 25. The offseason is just beginning, particularly in regard to free-agent hitters, few of which have signed while arms (Skubal, Rogers, Peralta, old friend Kris Bubic, Dustin May, Sonny Gray, Kaima Taira) dominate headlines. Perhaps my entire thesis is incorrect, and Kansas City always intended to trade for pitching then turn to free agency to fill holes in the lineup. But my hunch is the club sought to ink free agents to shore up most of its weaknesses (starting pitching, bullpen, left field, center field) and quickly learned the price of the buck had gone up on starting pitching. Damn tariffs. Either way, the next move to watch for is possibly a multi-year agreement with one of the impact hitters, such as left fielders Seiya Suzuki, Randy Arozarena, Ian Happ or Taylor Ward. Signing any of these four will, in all likelihood, cost much less both long-term and in 2027 than the crop of starting pitchers already off the board. The market dictated the direction of this early stage of the offseason, as it so often does. The Royals adjusted. Let’s give them some time before determining whether that pivot in approach will be rewarded.

item.content:encoded: 25% OFF We’re officially entering low power mode, but we have a couple more stories for you to close out the week. In the impending retail spirit, I review a device that’s a sex toy. You don’t really realize how much downtime there is in the song “Sandstorm” by Darude until you’re waiting for the bass to drop while it’s playing inside your vagina. In August 2025, I got an email with the subject line “‘Airpods for your @ss’ raises nearly half a million in Kickstarter campaign.” I get a lot of zany pitches for products that don’t exist yet, and a lot of pitches for products that do exist but perhaps should not. This one was for a device called the, a sex toy that turns music into vibration patterns. But the pitch didn’t include the phrase “sex toy” at all. Instead, it’s called an “internal music player.” I asked for a unit to review, expecting this to be purely conceptual. But they had one, and offered to send it. “The prototype functions very similarly to the final product but we do want to stress it’s a garage built prototype,” the rep for Groove Thing told me. I thought for a moment about putting something “garage built” and connected to a wall outlet into an orifice and passed. While, I decided to wait until the version they planned to send to customers in the fall was ready. The production-ready Groove Thing arrived at my doorstep last month in an intimidatingly large box. The configuration consists of a fairly hefty speaker that’s meant to sit on your nightstand, an AC power cable, and a “resonator base,” which connects to the speaker with a pinned cord. It also came with three attachment shapes: vaginal, anal, and external (a vac-u-lock adapter is available separately for attaching your own dildos to the base). The attachment shapes are made of hard plastic, not the soft, flexible silicone I’m used to in a sex toy. They lock onto the resonator with a twist. The Treasury Department's CIO is working very hard on... something.Jason writes: "As the Treasury Department dealt with the fallout of a hack that took down some of its services, its Chief Information Officer was pushing updates to Legatum, his vibe coded Civilization clone. Sam Corcos is the cofounder of the A16z-backed glucose monitoring health startup called Levels; He became the Treasury Department’s Chief Information Officer as a DOGE hire near the beginning of Trump’s second term, and has been a leading AI evangelist within the administration since. Corcos’s department is in charge of cybersecurity for the Treasury Department, and so it is possibly concerning that while the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is dealing with a “cybersecurity incident” that has taken a critical bank compliance reporting panel down, he has been actively pushing balance patches, new theme music for the Aztec faction, and critical tweaks to the in-game player assistance tooltips for Legatum, his vibe-coded 'turn-based strategy game in the tradition of Civilization VI.'"And this week’s podcast is out! We start this week with Joseph’s story about ARTEX, an AI hacking framework that is behind a bunch of breaches around the world. After the break, Google’s plan to have a 24/7 AI-powered TV channel that includes you as the main character. In the section for subscribers at the Supporter level, Matthew tells us how a data center being built is definitely not a data center.Get the pod wherever you listen.Sleepy times out here but let's give the internet a spin... Mayo Clinic must pay $906,088.88 in back wages to employees who handle scheduling, following an investigation into unpaid time; this includes the time they spend waiting for their computers to boot up. From CBS: Under the settlement, Mayo will no longer round time for these workers and will give them five minutes on the clock at the start of each day to boot up their computers. Mayo also agreed to continue policy changes it made during the investigation to make sure the workers are paid lawfully.A Carnegie Melon study found that partisan groups running ads posed as journalism outlets to sway elections. From CMU: "While these pink slime sites typically have no real ties to the local community they claim to cover, they publish a mixture of digitally generated local and national news. The harm, researchers say, rests in how these sites exploit people’s trust in local news to impact their beliefs. Also, as AI-generated content improves, more articles on pink slime sites appear to be written by real people even though they were manufactured by AI." Another platform takes an anti-AI stance, this time from music streaming platform Tidal: It's banning and mass-deleting tracks that are entirely AI generated. "43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, wrote on X. It's purging 29 million tracks, and the platform rejects between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day. “We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.” Andersen wrote, adding that 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. Alright, that's all from me for now. I have a pie to make.

item.title: I Listened to ‘Sandstorm’ Through a Sex Toy
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: You don’t really realize how much downtime there is in the song “Sandstorm” by Darude until you’re waiting for the bass to drop while it’s playing inside your vagina. In August 2025, I got an email with the subject line “‘Airpods for your @ss’ raises nearly half a million in Kickstarter campaign.” I get a lot of zany pitches for products that don’t exist yet, and a lot of pitches for products that do exist but perhaps should not. This one was for a device called the , a sex toy that turns music into vibration patterns. But the pitch didn’t include the phrase “sex toy” at all. Instead, it’s called an “internal music player.” I asked for a unit to review, expecting this to be purely conceptual. But they had one, and offered to send it. “The prototype functions very similarly to the final product but we do want to stress it’s a garage built prototype,” the rep for Groove Thing told me. I thought for a moment about putting something “garage built” and connected to a wall outlet into an orifice and passed. While , I decided to wait until the version they planned to send to customers in the fall was ready. The production-ready Groove Thing arrived at my doorstep last month in an intimidatingly large box. The configuration consists of a fairly hefty speaker that’s meant to sit on your nightstand, an AC power cable, and a “resonator base,” which connects to the speaker with a pinned cord. It also came with three attachment shapes: vaginal, anal, and external (a vac-u-lock adapter is available separately for attaching your own dildos to the base). The attachment shapes are made of hard plastic, not the soft, flexible silicone I’m used to in a sex toy. They lock onto the resonator with a twist. Opening the box and feeling the hard, inflexible plastic raised my skepticism that this thing would be comfortable. Most sex toys are covered in silky silicone that offers a little flexibility and give. But as I’m told over and over by the pamphlets that come in the box, Groove Thing “isn’t a vibrator.” Groove Thing inventor Michael Weiss-Malik, who co-founded it with Elizabeth Dell, told me it’s hard plastic for a reason, and is the result of testing feedback from the around 180 people they handed a prototype before putting it on the market.“We started with off-the-shelf silicone dongs, and they were already producing an interesting experience for people,” Weiss-Malik told me on a call. “But we experimented with different types of materials, and what we found was that the silicone transmitted way fewer ranges of frequencies than hard plastic, and the hard plastic produces much higher fidelity.” The mechanism that vibrates the base to the beat of the music is also different from most other sex toys on the market today, Weiss-Malik said. But he declined to share what actually runs the toy, beyond mysteriously stating it’s not “a motor.” Weiss-Malik is a former NASA engineer, where he worked on the software that helped map Mars. He’s also worked at Google, where he worked on Earth mapping software, and previously worked leadership roles at Uber and Cruise, the self-driving car company General Motors later acquired and ultimately shut down after a serious accident. But he’s been involved in the sex positive community in the San Francisco bay area “for going on 20 years,” he told me, and is the type of guy to pop into a sex shop anytime he passes one when traveling. All of this taken together makes a lot of sense to me, given that he’s the kind of guy to spend a summer between jobs tinkering in his garage, designing a device that could put music up your ass. “Groove Thing doesn't use a motor. We don't say what is in there, but it's not a motor,” he said. “It uses a different set of physics that's more similar to audio equipment, and as a result, it can actually reproduce a full sound form, not just an on-off. You know, a sound-responsive vibrator is mostly just an on-off switch that's connecting to the beat.” Other vibrating sex toys work in that way: An eccentric rotating mass motor spins, turning pre-programmed patterns into vibration. Handheld sex toy makers have to work around several factors, including the limits of these motors, the tendency of soft silicone to dampen vibration, and the shapes they need to compact them into to fit in a device that doesn’t wear out customers’ wrists. Groove Thing seems to get around some of these problems by skipping the typical rotating motor, shaping the attachments in such a way that you can insert them and then go mostly hands-free when lying down, and choosing a plastic that feels kind of awkward at first.The combination means different instruments and ranges come through as different levels of vibration. “A piano or bass guitar feels different than a drum kit. It almost feels like having a third ear,” Weiss-Malik said. “There's a level of fidelity there, where you have a whole new dimension to the sound that you're hearing. It works particularly well in bass, but it works all the way up to the mid frequencies.” Groove Thing replicates frequencies you can’t hear with your ears, he said — kind of like being at a concert and standing close enough to the stack that you feel it in your chest. As someone who recently almost lost their eyebrows and gained tinnitus at a Mogwai show, I get it, and I think for most people this comparison is what will make the Groove Thing click for them. ”Some of what you're feeling is subsonic; it's down below 20 hertz, and we actually reproduce that as well,” Weiss-Malik said. “So you actually experience parts of your music that you never even noticed were there before, or that your ears can't hear, and that at the very least, home stereo equipment has a very hard time reproducing. So you're getting an experience that hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of speakers are normally required for you to get that out of the recording.” This was my experience with “Sandstorm.” You wouldn’t believe how much not-music is going on in that song, but also, how the moments that seem like they should be intense rumbly bass-drops are actually at a higher register. The creators of Groove Thing want you to be able to play whatever you want, which you can from your phone via Bluetooth or the optional aux jack, but they also really, really want you to try their intro playlist, I assume to prevent people like myself from putting “Crab Rave” on the stereo and then writing it off as a bust. is eclectic, beginning with “Beads on the Wind: The Human Experience Remix” and “Aya,” which I would place in a repeat-Burning-Man-attendee genre (no judgement here), but continues into “Blinding Lights” by The Weeknd and, to my pleasant surprise, an underrated track from Taylor Swift’s album, “I Think He Knows.” An with more songs features mostly EDM but also throws “Piece of Me” by Britney Spears in there. This entire test run of this not-vibrator made me, an admittedly tone deaf and musically unsophisticated person (see the previous lines), realize how much is happening in music that I’m never picking up with my own two ears. The “third ear” analogy is pretty spot-on: To enjoy the Groove Thing with an open mind, you have to let go of the typical expectations of other sex tech. Climax isn’t the point. The point is to use your junk to go on a musical journey, which is something that will resonate strongly for some, and miss others. “You know, people don’t go to a concert just to hear the finale and go home. Groove Thing isn’t a tool like most vibrators are,” Weiss-Malik told me. “It's more like a concert experience. You get to bask in pleasure for a period of time. In our early beta tester groups, most people who had unlimited usage of it used it for over an hour in their first session. Most of the second time users in that beta group also used it for over an hour in their second session.” The entire sex tech market has been trending away from the literal, anatomical, and climax-centered for years, with more toys coming in abstracted colors, shapes, and features that focus on pleasure and experience over getting your own personal money shot. I see Groove Thing as a logical step in that evolution.Groove Thing is shipping out orders as of this month, and retails at $369 for the single unit and more for add-ons and additional units for partnered play.

item.title: It’s Never Too Late To Be The Best Band In The World Again
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: We begin at Webster Hall in New York City. I'm standing on the main floor with the rest of the general admission patrons. My best friend Howard is with me. He's been waiting nearly as many years as I have for what's about to transpire. So has everyone else in the room. Many of them are already drunk. Many more are still queued up in the line at the merch stand, which has run out of at least one line of T-shirts and will likely run out of others.Howard and I are soaking in the pre-concert playlist playing over the loudspeakers, and waiting for the lights to go dark. I've put in my earplugs. I can't hear anything Howard says, but it doesn't matter. He's ready. I'm ready. Everyone is ready, because we're about to witness the resurrection of Sugar, one of the greatest bands of the 1990s. None of us believed this band would reunite. Never considered the possibility, really. Shit, prior to tonight I didn't even think the members of Sugar—guitarist/vocalist Bob Mould, bassist David Barbe, drummer Malcolm Travis—had considered the idea themselves. For Mould, the ringleader, Sugar wasn't even the most famous band he'd played in. The fact that they're here together on this opening night of the "Love You Even Still" tour, and that we're all here to witness it, feels like a happy fluke.But this is no fluke at all. This is a reunion that required many years, plus a well-timed video birthday card, to become a reality. I have seen Mould on his own in concert more times than I can count, but I've never seen him take the stage live with Travis and Barbe. That's because I discovered Sugar's music a beat too late. They had already broken up before my roommate put on their second album, File Under: Easy Listening, in our college dorm room. Once I heard the opening chords to "Gee Angel," I knew right away that Sugar was my band. That they would be my band. If I never got to see them in the flesh, so be it. The music had me forever. I knew it back in 1997, and I still know it today, 29 years later.

item.title: Your guide to having tough conversations this holiday season.
item.author: SRS0=C+a8=JO=mail135.sea51.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295094-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: We are a deeply polarized people. Social media makes it easy for us to surround ourselves with people who feel and act the same way. Our relationships with family and friends are unique in that we’re bonded socially for reasons often beyond our political and social values. This might mean you’re confronted with conversations you haven’t had the chance to practice before. Or, you may have watched people online host them without an attempt to stay in relationship – like a takedown video on TikTok that doesn’t leave room for repair.As you engage with your community this holiday season, here are some tools to navigate tough conversations. Remember, all of these are only suggestions; relationships are unique and complex, and these best practices might not be best for you. I hope that they help you feel grounded and resourced to say the hard thing, share your point of view, and listen to others. Even if it feels futile, trying to bridge the divide between you and someone else is part of the work of forging togetherness on a larger scale. Here’s where to start.Often, confrontation isn’t as effective as a nuanced conversation about a tricky topic. Consider leading a generative conversation by leading with your feelings, using “I” statements, and being vulnerable about your own journey with the topic(s) at hand. Please note: if calling someone out is a more direct and straightforward way to start the conversation and feels more generative to you, please do so.Start from a place of empowerment.We all have the tools to dismantle oppression and reimagine spaces for all of us to thrive. You can start conversations with that mindset, which will enable your audience to see themselves as part of the solution, and not just the problem. You can say things like, “What can we do together?” “What tools do we have as a family?” “How can we show up best in our neighborhood?”Don’t wait for something to react to.Most of the work regarding dismantling white supremacy happens as a reaction to a single incident. But for this work to be sustainable, we – especially those with privilege – need to get comfortable with the discomfort of this work proactively, not just as a reaction. Bring it up directly, perhaps by naming how a recent interaction made you feel.There is no such thing as the “best” time.Many people are hesitant to get into tough conversations during the holidays, a time that can feel precious and “distanced” from the tension of everyday life. But there’s rarely a “best” time for difficult conversations. Consider instead: how can I host this conversation in the most generative way at this moment? How can I start this conversation now to create more space for it in the future?Center whiteness, not Blackness (or other marginalized identities).When discussing racism specifically, many try to defend or validate marginalized communities. But as you do, don’t forget to name the harm of whiteness and colonization, not just those harms. When we focus the conversation on harmful actions, it leads more directly to changing these actions, not just building empathetic ties.For example, this can look like naming the ongoing oppression led by the Israeli state when discussing Palestine. Or, naming the ongoing oppression the U.S. places on the Indigenous communities here.Remember, no community needs to be validated by another to “deserve” respect. We all deserve respect. We need to adjust our actions and recognize our shortcomings to provide it, and reckon with the harm being caused.You might want to start this conversation for a variety of reasons. Perhaps you want to see more accountability, or you simply want your family to know how their words and actions make you feel. Take a moment to honor what you’d like to see come out of this conversation, and you can even share that openly as the conversation progresses.Hold your loved ones accountable. Ensure that you’re no longer tolerating their statements. Note how their continued racism will affect your relationship, and be prepared to stand firm. Remember that accountability is a practice of love, and so is setting boundaries for you and yours.Demonstrate the actions you’ve taken to dismantle white supremacy in your own life. Use examples of what you’ve learned and unlearned in your own education. Be vulnerable about where you’re still growing – because we all have space to improve! And note how else you’re moving forward.If you feel resourced, you can use this time to invite this person to join in – perhaps by reading a book together, having further discussions, etc. If that’s not available to you at the moment, you can offer to check in with them later to see how they’re progressing. Consider sharing a TikTok video you saw recently, or recommending a topical video for your family to watch.Tough conversations with loved ones are not easy. If you have the opportunity, make a self-care plan for before, during, and after. Beforehand, practice some deep breathing and grounding exercises. Remember to check in with your breath and body during the conversation. And, plan for some time to decompress afterward, whether that’s scheduling time to decompress with a friend or therapist, taking a long walk later, journaling, etc. It might also be helpful to write some talking points and goals beforehand to help you feel more comfortable.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers Benched For First And Possibly Final Time
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Aaron Rodgers will not start the Pittsburgh Steelers' next game, the team announced late Tuesday night. Curiously late, actually, and in a manner that reeks of intrigue. Nothing Rodgers does is normal, so why should the potential end of his NFL career be?Mike McCarthy was unequivocal about it on Monday: "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback," he said, when asked about making a change one day after a loss to the Eagles that featured Rodgers putting up one of the feeblest halves of QB play in 20 years. Something must have changed, and quickly. "After a series of meetings," as Adam Schefter put it, "'some good, some bad,'" the call was made. It "was a coach's decision," ESPN reports. At 11:10 p.m. Tuesday, an odd time for an announcement, the Steelers put out a statement from a team spokesperson, an odd source for a personnel decision, that Rodgers will be in street clothes for Friday's game.

item.title: Trump’s new, dumb plan to stymie congressional subpoenas
item.author: delivery_20261125061502.48601725.7339@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
We’re releasing this week’s one day early so as not to interrupt your Thanksgiving holiday. We also have some important announcements about the newsletter at the bottom of the page. Thanks, as ever, for reading! Last week, President Donald Trump pulled out his favorite Sharpie to do what he does best: sign an executive order awarding himself unprecedented power that will result in a nasty legal fight. This latest order has to do with executive privilege and attempts to shield all communications between the White House and federal agencies and contractors from the incoming Democratic congressional majorities who have pledged to investigate the Trump administration. It’s a transparent attempt to thwart congressional oversight into the administration’s numerous dealings, ranging from the White House ballroom project to violent immigration enforcement practices to the ongoing upheaval at Nvidia. The order is classic Trump, setting up the legal groundwork to push back against Congress’ authority in order to protect himself and his allies. However, like many of the executive orders signed during his second term, this latest one tees up a larger constitutional question about the extent of executive branch privilege versus congressional control. Ultimately, the outcome is unlikely to favor the president.
“In order to protect and serve the American people, the executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without fear that confidential information will be released to unauthorized third parties,” is how the president kicked off his executive order. It goes on to claim that Congress can’t seek information from executive branch departments, agencies, employees, or contractors “without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions.” The order ends by demanding that federal employees and contractors notify and coordinate with the White House if they receive requests for information related to congressional investigations. If they don’t comply, they can expect contracts to be terminated and could even face debarment—a blacklist that prevents them from ever getting a government contract again.
This executive order is a culmination of recent Trump administration attempts to mount a counterattack on the incoming Democratic-majority Congress. It started when a U.S. attorney in Texas sent out a slew of letters to members of Congress accusing them of engaging in unlawful activity after they pledged to investigate the administration. Then, last week, White House counsel Will Scharf issued a directive to all federal agencies stipulating that they get “approval” from the White House before agreeing to appear before any congressional committee. The last act came out Friday in the form of this new executive order.
“This desperate Executive Order is totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful. Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars, not Trump’s personal billions (made illegally on the side),” the House Judiciary Committee account posted on X. “Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs.”
While the White House is attempting to assert the doctrine of executive privilege over any and all communications between the executive branch and federal employees and contractors it hires, this isn’t historically how executive privilege has worked. It is a constitutionally protected right, defined as the president’s ability to withhold documents or information in their possession or in possession of the executive branch from the legislative or judicial branches of government. The Supreme Court has affirmed that it’s necessary in order to allow the president to carry out their duties and be free to discuss issues candidly without fear that the deliberations could be made public. Up until this point, as Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney for Alabama, recently noted, executive privilege has been understood to protect limited internal deliberations, “not commercial dealings between the government and contractors using public money.”
The extent of executive privilege was famously put to the test during the Watergate scandal, when former Republican President Richard Nixon’s White House faced a criminal indictment. Nixon argued that his recorded conversations with his staff should be covered by executive privilege, thereby shielding him from a federal subpoena. The Supreme Court disagreed, concluding that neither the doctrine of separation of powers nor the executive branch’s need for confidentiality justified absolute presidential privilege, with limited exceptions for military or diplomatic affairs. The decision has remained untouched ever since, with executive privilege understood to not supersede “the fundamental demands of due process of law in the fair administration of justice.”
While the White House is pressure testing executive privilege in the context of congressional investigations, it has also been using this strategy in the ongoing litigation over the future of the Kennedy Center. In that case, when lawyers for Ohio Rep. Joyce Beatty attempted to get the Trump administration to hand over dozens of emails and text messages between White House aides, the president’s legal team argued that its communications should be granted executive privilege in order to protect the White House’s ability to speak candidly and confidentially with staff. Judge Christopher R. Cooper, appointed by the Obama administration, is overseeing this case and has indicated an inclination to decide that some but not all of the president’s communications should be protected. It will come down to the context of the conversations: Were they about policy related to the Kennedy Center or about the “color of carpets”?
The administration’s right to executive privilege will weigh against Congress’ right to oversight, and there is plenty of case law and federal law that support Congress’ authority to check the executive branch. Consider the 1967 case , when the Supreme Court affirmed that Congress’ oversight power “comprehends probes into departments of the Federal Government to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste,” concluding that “motives alone would not vitiate an investigation which had been instituted by a House of Congress if that assembly’s legislative purpose is being served.”
There’s also the 1975 case Eastland v. United States Servicemen’s Fund, in which SCOTUS similarly concluded that “in determining the legitimacy of a congressional act we do not look to the motives alleged to have prompted it.” This all boils down to how the courts have long made clear that the relevant question isn’t why Congress is investigating a certain issue; “it’s solely whether the investigation has an objectively legitimate purpose,” Steve Vladeck, a law professor at Georgetown University, explained in his One First newsletter.
Last time we checked, investigating potential acts of executive branch corruption, like if donors to Trump’s ballroom project received deferential treatment, and violations of federal law, which include if the Epstein files were publicly released according to the Epstein Files Transparency Act, squarely fall under a legitimate legislative purpose.
It’s also worth mentioning that there are numerous federal laws that protect federal employees’ right to speak with Congress. The Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912 guarantees federal employees the right to directly share information with Congress without interference or denial; Congress passed the act after the Roosevelt administration tried to ban federal employees from speaking with the legislative body unless they went through a federal agency department head. Without it, as Iowa Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley aptly explained back in 2018, “we would have an aristocratic government, one that would be dominated by the executive branch.” Incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee Maggie Hassan warned federal contractors that the president’s executive order “does not override their obligation to comply with congressional requests for information or subpoenas.” We’ll have to wait and see how the fight over executive privilege plays out, at least until the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, and Democrats can officially begin their investigations and issue subpoenas. They’ll have two years to accomplish their accountability agenda, and now, with Trump’s latest order, they may need to bake in time for lengthy legal fights. “This new EO, dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies, is nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption,” Lisa Gilbert, co-president of the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said in a statement. “It will not succeed. Sunlight is coming, and corrupt administration insiders and contractors, both, will have to face the American people.”

item.title: Trump's ICE Sent Thousands of Recruits Out After Training Them Online
item.author: Andre Costa
item.content:encoded: The Trump regime let more than 3,500 ICE recruits skip a month of in-person training and do their basic training online instead, a 19-page draft report by the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general found. More than 80% of them finished the online modules within ten days, more than 10% in under 24 hours and at least five in about two hours. The New York Times obtained the draft, which has not been finalised or made public, on Friday.The recruits who did their training online all had previous law enforcement experience, and they were part of nearly 6,000 officers who got reduced training between August 2025 and July 2026. ICE cut academy instruction for more than 2,000 recruits with no police background from about 543 hours to roughly 300, taking hours from firearms, arrest procedures and driving. It also scrapped the two-attempt limit on a training test, and one officer needed 32 attempts to pass. Nearly 90% of the ICE officials running on-the-job training who answered the watchdog's questionnaire said that training was "not successful", and one ICE instructor called the overhaul a "catastrophic failure".Kristi Noem, then Homeland Security Secretary, and her senior adviser Corey Lewandowski strongly backed the changes, and ICE's former training chief told investigators he was ordered to make them. Trump ousted Noem in March. Her successor, Markwayne Mullin, restored stricter requirements in July, but the draft says ICE "has not fully addressed training gaps born of the reductions and revisions" for the officers it had already sent out.The shortcuts fed the regime's hiring drive for its mass deportation campaign. ICE announced on 3 January that it had hired more than 12,000 officers and agents in under a year, more than doubling its force from about 10,000 to 22,000, paid for with $8 billion from Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and $50,000 signing bonuses. On 22 January the department claimed that all new ICE students attend the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center and "meet the same high standards ICE has always required". More than 3,500 of them were doing it online.ICE officer David Brouillette was one of the experienced hires. He joined late in 2025 and on 13 July shot dead Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian father with a pending asylum case and a work permit, during a vehicle stop in Biddeford, Maine. Guerrero was not the man ICE had a warrant for. Because Brouillette had worked as a police officer at a Veterans Affairs medical centre, ICE skipped him past the training centre and gave him a virtual course followed by field use-of-force training. Two former wives have accused him of abuse, a Maine judge ordered him to give up his guns in 2019, and he denies the allegations. Maine has not charged him.Federal agents in Minneapolis shot dead Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother, on 7 January, and Alex Pretti, an intensive care nurse, on 24 January, both of them US citizens. ICE and CBP had killed or let die 97 people since January 2025 by the end of October, a count the Crust News team keeps on the ICE List at theicelist.org. The draft did not examine whether the training cuts played a part in any of those deaths.Inspector General Joseph Cuffari's office condemned the release of the draft, saying such disclosures "undermine the integrity of the oversight process". ICE said "a significant portion of officers brought on during the hiring surge have law enforcement experience and have already successfully completed a law enforcement academy". Mullin told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that "there were some decisions that were made before I was secretary that we are having to undo".The draft says ICE has still not closed the training gaps left in the thousands of officers it hired under Noem's rules.

item.title: Treasury CIO Is Vibe Coding a ‘Civilization’ Clone During Treasury Department Hack
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: As the Treasury Department dealt with the fallout of a hack that took down some of its services, its Chief Information Officer was pushing updates to , his vibe coded Civilization clone. is similar to “on purpose,” according to a readme on Corcos’s Github. “If you have played you already know the basics: found cities, pick research, queue production, fight on hexes […] Legatum is built largely with AI coding agents [both Claude and OpenAI’s Codex], and all of its art is AI-generated. Most of the art comes from OpenAI's image models through ChatGPT.” is also open source, and has been getting updated in real time while I am writing this article and after a notice went up on the FinCEN website that said it was “investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.”While newer AI models can do a lot on their own and can often work for hours or days without much human intervention, shoddy or lazy prompting by Corcos has resulted in a situation where Claude is pushing updates that come as the result of direct feedback from Corcos about improvements that can be made to the game. Some of the most recent updates include direct quotes from Corcos about how he’s feeling about the game, indicating that he is actively involved in its development. One of the most recent updates, pushed after the FinCEN hack, includes, for example, a new special unit for Egypt, which came at the explicit direction of Corcos. “I like Chariot archers for egypt, their current special unit is lame,” Corcos told Claude. That update was pushed while a Treasury Department website displayed a warning noting that “as a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.”“FinCEN is working diligently to return all systems to normal operations as soon as possible,” FinCEN added. Luckily, players will not have to wait any longer for more faction-appropriate music as Corcos and his AI have been working diligently to improve the game’s “production value,” according to a Github commit pushed after midnight on Wednesday. This new update includes “Music by era, the Aztecs' own music, the sea, and gunpowder-age battle sounds.”Crucially, players can play in a web browser: “Nothing to install.” Something you can’t do in a web browser, at the moment, is reliably file certain compliance documents about the Banking Secrecy Act with the Treasury Department; “FinCEN is extending deadlines for filers impacted by the disruption,” it said. I did play for several minutes in my web browser but then got bored and decided to go searching through Corcos’s GitHub instead.After this article was published, a Treasury Department spokesperson directed me to a tweet by Corcos in which he said autonomous agents are pushing the updates (which is obvious). Corcos did not address the fact that the agents are acting on his direct feedback.“It's built by autonomous SI agents that plan, write, test and merge code on their own at all hours of the day. While I am at work, it runs on my home computer. The GitHub activity is agents committing, not me at a keyboard,” he wrote. “This is a side project that has been running continuously for a few weeks. It runs entirely on my personal accounts: Claude and ChatGPT subscriptions I pay for myself, plus my own AWS and Cloudflare. No taxpayer money or government resources.”

item.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 75: Andrew Tuttle & Darren Cross

item.content:encoded: On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, Bob Holmes of the ambient country band SUSS has Andrew Tuttle & Darren Cross on the show to talk about their new release . Hailing from Australia, Andrew and Darren are experimental musicians whose banjo and acoustic guitar collaborations stretch the boundaries of ambient Americana. They also bring along a playlist of new instrumental music from their homeland including Lawrence English, Jordan Ireland, Monica Brooks, and more.For Flow State we’re mostly off this week but today we’re listening to two Tuttle records, including . Tuttle (based in Brisbane) and Cross (in Sydney) play banjo and acoustic guitar / synth respectively, and both contribute to effects and mixing. The compositions are airy, the synths creating a big space for the banjo and guitar to resonate and linger. We’re also playing Tuttle’s 2022 record, , which foregrounds the banjo and features Cross on two tracks.Have a great rest of your week.
