item.title: University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a .During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.“It is widely promoted as the next step in furthering novel research taking place at this University. What is conveniently left out on flyers and pamphlets is that this is only part of the proposition, 10% in fact, the other 90% is being used by Los Alamos — a nuclear weapons developer,” a sophomore studying biochemistry told the board before the vote. “We already have three existing high tech data centers used for research. Why must we push forward with another one that is promoting nuclear warfare?”An electrician from Ypsilanti Township, a representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) union, supported the construction project. “This will create 300 plus jobs for our members, all local, [and] give back to the community,” he said. “IBEW is in favor of the data center, excuse me, ‘high compute research center.’”People who attended the regent’s meeting to discuss other topics referenced the vote during their presentations. “You voted today to fund a $785 million data center project in Ypsilanti, much to the opposition of the residents of the area, acting against what many residents in the area are calling environmental racism. I think I can speak for many students when I say I am frankly appalled by this decision,” a student who was there to discuss carbon emissions said.A library worker present to talk about how the University treats its workers invoked the data center. “I’m not sure I can confidently appeal to your sense of compassion around this. The officials and residents of Ypsi Township are saying ‘stop,’ saying ‘no,’ saying ‘this hurts.’ And you and others responsible for this nuclear weapons data center project have shown you don’t care about the basic issue of consent as you plow ahead,” he said.Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.Despite the opposition in the room, the regents approved the project. “It’s been very controversial [...] For me, this is all about an investment in the community and it’s an investment, in many different ways,” regent Denise Ilitch said just before the vote. “The community will be enhanced — they may not feel it now, some, but I venture to say that there will be much good that will come from this.”Many in Ypsilanti Township disagree. After the regents voted, the leadership and residents of the Township gathered for a panel discussion about the data center. One of the speakers that night was Jay Coghlan, the executive director of Nuclear Watch of New Mexico, a watchdog group that tracks Los Alamos. “The data center issue here in Ypsilanti is unique in that it is the clearest example of the pending merger of AI and nuclear weapons, which doesn’t bode well,” Coghlan told 404 Media.Coghlan told 404 Media that he shared the Township’s concerns about how the data center will use water and electricity but said he thinks its construction will have farther reaching consequences. “Our nation is transforming from the military-industrial complex that Eisenhower warned us about to a Silicon Valley-Pentagon-Wall Street complex that closely links economics, economic inequality, increasing militarism, and I dare say the rise of techno-fascism,” he said.U of M has repeatedly said the data center will mostly be used to power medical breakthroughs and conduct cancer research, something it’s highlighted in flyers and pamphlets it’s mailed to people in the Township. LANL to the people of the community in September that promised it wouldn't build nuclear weapons in their backyard. “I'm going ‘Duh, yeah, you're not going to bring plutonium to Ypsilanti in Michigan,” Coghlan said. “But I expect this data center to have a lot to do with the design of new nuclear weapons. So, in that way, Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.”Coghlan said he finds hope in the opposition to the project. “I’m very impressed by the intensity of opposition that I have witnessed. There seems to be a pretty widespread public awareness of the data center in Ypsilanti, Township.”During the Township meeting on November 19, after the regents voted, Ypsilanti Township attorney Douglas Winters said he was mad. “What did we learn on November 3rd? Two weeks ago and two days, voters around this country loudly declared that they were sick and tired of government corruption. They were tired of secrecy. They were tired of abuse of power. They were tired of threats to democracy and the disregard of governmental accountability. And, importantly, they also said they were sick and tired of these data centers,” he said. “Somehow that message did not make it to Ann Arbor. That message did not make it to the board of regents.”Winters and other leaders vowed to keep fighting the data center’s construction. In May, the community’s water authority voted to restrict new construction on infrastructure to data center projects while it conducts a review of their impact on the Township’s water supply. The University called the move “unlawfully discriminatory.” In August, the Township passed a six month moratorium on new electrical infrastructure, a move aimed at delaying the project.

item.title: It’s Josh Johnson Time In The NFL
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: He's back! He's back, he's back, he's freaking BACK! The Josh Johnson's Race Against Time Netflix series is surely just around the corner, and all Johnson needs to get it over is land one more gig before retirement so that he can become the first player to play for half the teams in his chosen sport.We have visited the topic of Johnson's peripatetic journey through professional football before, with our first celebration dating all the way back to the dying embers of the COVID era. Johnson has come and gone as needed and as usual since, and the only reason to re-dredge this particular part of the bay is that Johnson started and finished Sunday's Arizona Cardinals game at Kansas City. It went about the way it should; the Cardinals are punting the season, and got punted in turn by the Chiefs, 34-7. Nobody seemed overly troubled by either the game play or the ensuing numbers, because nobody was under the illusion that this was an especially meaningful game.That very much includes the Cardinals. They are uniquely awful because they are ritually awful; having to start four quarterbacks in four weeks is some deeply and unmistakably Cardinals Stuff. That they have reached the Josh Johnson stage of their season this early is fairly Cardinals as well, but less novel. There, at least, they have plenty of company.

item.title: Jensen Huang Returns To Nvidia After Mr. Market Deems Him Too Indispensable
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: Two weeks after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to admit to having conducted one of his many multiply illicit affairs with a woman accused of working as a spy for the Chinese government, 11 days after he was forced out of his position at the titanic chipmaker and tentpole of the world economy, and one week after I made a pilgrimage to the holy site in Silicon Valley where he came up with the idea for the multi-trillion dollar company, Jensen Huang is back. The Nvidia board announced on Monday morning that he would return to his position, reassuring the public and Nvidia investors that Huang's "reinstatement poses no national security risk."Momentum had been building toward Huang's reinstatement since he was forced out. The strongest push reportedly has come from within Nvidia, which might seem somewhat surprising, given reports of Huang having "terrorized" and "humiliated" staffers who annoyed him or otherwise got in his way. Concerning as those reports may be, they don't really matter when considered against the credit Huang popularly receives for how much money Nvidia has made for everyone. The myth of the lone visionary CEO is largely a marketing fiction, but in the case of Nvidia, which has flirted with a $5 trillion market cap, it's more or less true. Huang created a corporate architecture that gave him an unusual amount of power, and he used it to make a series of risky and ultimately very successful bets. This is why so many current and former Nvidia people called on the board to Stand With Jensen.As for the people opposed to Huang's return, some of them are AI people who find themselves on the opposite side of Huang in the debate over closed vs. open models. Huang has long argued for AI development that favors open-source–style knowledge sharing over the closed-off frontier lab model, a stance that makes sense, given that the open model of development creates the largest and hungriest possible market for his company's chips. The frontier lab model's argument against this mode is that the political-religious stakes in the race to create the machine god before everybody else are just too high to allow for anything as squishy as sharing; as with Huang's case, that argument neatly aligns with their business interests.

item.title: The movies of 2015
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: I absolutely love movie mashups. Once nice aspect of a decade-old one is that by now I've seen a bunch of the relevant movies, and even a 2-second excerpt is enough to bring back pleasant memories.I also use mashups to quickly scout for movies that might be of interest. If you see a scene in the video and want to identify the movie, make a note of the time stamp and then look it up on this list.I don't know how these are created; how does someone get access to so much material? Then it requires a modicum of artistic vision to link the segments in various coherent ways. I'll never have that skill or those resources, but perhaps TYWKIWDBI is in a way a "mashup" itself.

item.title: A Shooting Slump Spells Celtic Doom
item.author: Giri Nathan
item.content:encoded: The Boston Celtics opened the season 11-2, and everything looked green and healthy. Jayson Tatum slid back back into his perpetual "No. 4 in MVP voting" status, newly added Paul George was hooping as if de-aged, and head coach Joe Mazzulla's offensive philosophy looked unimpeachable (despite having often invited impeachment in postseasons past). Put the defense in rotation, find an open three, and the math will carry you to victory. Through those first 13 games, it really did. The Celtics were throwing up 43 threes a game (fifth-most in the league) and making them at 38.5 percent clip (fourth-best in the league). They looked cleaner and sharper than they did in last year's Jaylen Brown-led campaign, an even purer distillation of Mazzulla ball.Maybe that should have prepared fans to confront an even purer dark side of Mazzulla ball, too. Since then, the Celtics have screeched into a four-game skid: hosting the Orlando Magic, then losing on the road to the Denver Nuggets, Sacramento Kings, and Golden State Warriors by 10 points, 4 points, 1 point, and 1 point, respectively. That's cause for alarm, given that this team hasn't lost four games in a row since May 2021. Sunday's 88-87 loss to a Warriors team led in scoring by Brandin Podziemski, Gui Santos, and Charles Bassey was particularly gruesome. The Celtics led for most of the second half, but still went on to lose the game, despite the Warriors failing to score a point in the final two minutes and 30 seconds of regulation. Tatum was 0-of-7 in the second half, including an attempted game-winner over Draymond Green from the elbow. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kokqvX02DLc

item.title: "Howcatchem" explained
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: I encountered "howcatchem" for the first time this past week, I think in a word puzzle somewhere. Had to look it up, and found the answer in Wikipedia:"An inverted detective story, occasionally known as a "reverse whodunnit" or "howcatchem", is a crime fiction structure in which the commission of the crime is shown or described at the beginning, usually including the identity of the perpetrator. The story then describes the detective's attempt to solve the mystery. There may also be subsidiary puzzles, such as why the crime was committed, which are explained or resolved during the story. This format is the opposite of the more typical "whodunit", in which all of the details of the perpetrator of the crime are not revealed until the story's climax. The first such story was R. Austin Freeman's The Case of Oskar Brodski published in Pearson's Magazine in 1912. The television series is one of the best-known examples of this genre."Multiple famous examples are cited at the link.

item.title: Tarik Skubal’s Huge Mets Deal May Be The Last Of Its Kind
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: Hey, at least it wasn't the Dodgers. It was, however, the other, generally less frightening team you might have expected: Jon Heyman reported Sunday afternoon that Tarik Skubal would be signing with the New York Mets. ESPN's Jeff Passan followed up to say that Skubal's contract will be worth $450 million over nine years, rocketing past Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million contract for the most expensive pitching contract in MLB history by total value.The best comparison for Skubal is not Yamamoto but Gerrit Cole, who signed a nine-year, $324 million contract with the New York Yankees back in 2019, which, with some very hasty back-of-the-napkin inflation math, was worth around the same value as Skubal's contract today. At the time that Cole signed the contract, he was 29, a year younger than Skubal now, and though he had yet to win a Cy Young at that point in his career, Cole ranked in the top five in voting in each of the previous two years. With two years now remaining on Cole's contract, reasonable and unreasonable Yankees fans alike would mostly agree that even after he lost a year and change to Tommy John surgery, the sum total of Cole's contract will turn out to have been worth it: the 2023 Cy Young award, solid postseason starts, likely no truly unplayable years through the end of his contract, and spanning enough time for the Yankees' beard rule to be repealed while he was still with the team.If Skubal's contract plays out as well as Cole's, even Tommy John–inclusive and beard rule–exclusive, then by heuristic, it will have been a successful contract for the Mets. There are more obvious confounding factors for Skubal than there were at the time of Cole's contract: Skubal is a year older and, earlier this season, missed time to remove a "loose body" from his elbow. Ideally a starting pitcher would have all their bodies fixed in place; some number of those bodies being loose amounts to a negative indicator for long-term health. And while Cole's first season with the Yankees was shortened due to a global pandemic that nobody could have predicted when he signed on Dec. 18, 2019, Skubal's contract comes just over a week before baseball's collective bargaining agreement will expire; it is increasingly unlikely, as owners continue pushing for a salary cap and floor and a lockout appears ever more inevitable, that Skubal's first season will be a complete one.

item.title: Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You’ll Be the Main Character
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the <user_profile>. The generated customized video follows the style and format of the <top_ watches> of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the <preferred_genres> of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The <top watches> and <preferred _genres> parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says. The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.” The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+. AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea. As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.

item.title: Max Verstappen Couldn’t Pass Up A Chance To Bully George Russell
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: While both the Drivers' and Constructors' Championships are done and dusted in the 2026 Formula 1 season—the former thanks to almost-child Kimi Antonelli's majestic season, and the latter also thanks to his Mercedes teammate George Russell—there are still important storylines to be sorted out, which now include the continuation of F1's most compelling psychodrama, featuring Russell and Max Verstappen.Late on Saturday night, Verstappen did what he has done in all but one of the Las Vegas Grand Prix races since it debuted in 2023: He won. Verstappen is now 3-for-4 on the Strip, only losing out in 2024 to, of all people, Russell. That part isn't particularly relevant, but it's a fun quirk to this rivalry that has become heated once more. During free practice on Friday, Verstappen overtook Russell ahead of a push lap, and when Russell tried to take the position back on the inside, the pair collided, essentially ruining that practice lap for both.This infuriated Russell, who said that while "there's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap," a move like Verstappen's can screw over the other driver. He went on to say that Verstappen does this all the time, to a lot of drivers, and that he's had enough of it. "Everybody accepts it, and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

item.title: A Wild Week at One Royal Way
item.author: SRS0=OXl3=JM=mg-d1.substack.com=bounce+5f4299.39b08c6-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: I didn’t have the Royals pegged as the team that would make the first big splash in the trade market this off-season, but that’s exactly what happened last Wednesday. Early that morning reports started circulating that JJ Picollo was dangling former All-Star 3B Maikel Garcia in trade talks to bolster their pitching staff for 2027.Public opinion about the deal among both KC and Seattle fans on social media was all over the place …I love the deal, with one caveat we’ll discuss in a minuteAfter the deal was announced, some of the local radio talking heads said that even the Royals had grown weary of Garcia’s questionable work ethic and effort level on the field. I’m not sure Garcia’s on-field performance in Kansas City was all that either. Yes, he had a terrific 2025 season. The Royals should have traded him a year ago when his value was as high as it likely will ever be. Instead, JJ Picollo gave Garcia a $52M contract extension and we all watched him struggle through a very bad and injury-plagued 2026 season.Garcia obviously provided excellent defense at third base, and that will not be easy to replace. The point is that Garcia’s body of work with the bat is not what a lot of Royals fans seem to think. It will be fascinating to see how he does in Seattle’s notoriously poor hitting ballpark.Let’s look at the other two players the Royals gave up, as well as the three they received from Seattle…In addition to Garcia Seattle gets…Of course you can’t assume a guy who hasn’t pitched above High A is going to exert the same kind of dominance in the majors, but fastballs like Langevin’s don’t grow on trees folks. It’s a sign of JJ Picollo’s urgency to win in 2027 that a reliever-starved organization traded their best relief prospect for some immediate help.Seattle thought highly enough of Ferrer to trade their 2021 first round draft pick (Harry Ford) for him a year ago. My favorite description of Ferrer so far…”He’s like Angel Zerpa if Zerpa was good at pitching”.Kudos to JJ for recognizing that it made sense to move Garcia, but I sure wish he could have gotten it done without involving Langevin.Not gonna lie, this one hurts. Izzy has long been a DC favorite, dating all the way back to the 2021 Pre-Season Manifesto where I predicted he would be the AL Rookie of the Year. Isbel broke camp with the big club that spring, but hit his way back to Omaha and only played in 28 big league games. Since that time Isbel has been the quasi-regular center fielder. His defense has always been elite, but the bat just never blossomed like we all hoped. He finishes his KC career with a .235/.284/.357 slash line. Ultimately I think the on base percentage did him in.I don’t think that Roccaforte is going to just be given the every day job in CF, but the free agent market is pretty slim. I’ve seen some speculation that the Royals could bring back Lane Thomas to platoon with Rocco. I don’t hate that idea.The Royals still have a glaring need for a RH impact bat in the outfield, and they only have 8 days to get something done before a labor lockout is imposed on Dec. 2nd. Could be another wild week in store at One Royal Way. Let me know in the comments what you think about the Garcia trade!

item.title: Malian music
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: From reader soubriquet's blog Grit in the Gears comes this delightful videoThe musicians are Ali Farka Toure - Ali Ibrahim “Farka” Touré (October 31, 1939 – March 7, 2006) was a Malian singer and multi-instrumentalist, and one of the African continent’s most internationally renowned musicians. His music is widely regarded as representing a point of intersection of traditional Malian music and its North American cousin, the blues. The belief that the latter is historically derived from the former is reflected in Martin Scorsese’s often quoted characterization of Touré’s tradition as constituting "the DNA of the blues". Touré was ranked number 76 on Rolling Stone’s list of “The 100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time” and number 37 on Spin magazine's "100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time". -and Abdoulaye Diabaté. I don't know what proportion of this piece is traditional Malian. The language (Tuareg) certainly, the melody and rhythms probably. But what fascinates me is how the incorporation of modern instrumentation and electronic modulation makes the music more "accessible" to my ear. Not sure you'll like it? Give it a click to start up while you scroll further down the blog.

item.title: Dylan Larkin Déménage À Montréal
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: After an agonizingly long trade-demand/suspension saga that featured the former Red Wings captain fully abandoning his team a month into this season, Dylan Larkin has received his wish—mostly. As one of Kash Patel's good buddies, the disgruntled Detroiter was reportedly wielding his no-movement clause to keep the Wings from resolving his situation with a Canadian team. But a few weeks without playing hockey (or getting paid) apparently softened his stance. Larkin will be suiting up for the division rival Montreal Canadiens, and in return, Wings interim GM Shawn Horcoff got a bushel of draft picks, a backup goalie at best in Sam Montembeault, a draft-bust depth forward in Kirby Dach, and a real prospect in Michael Hage.If it feels like the Habs won this trade, it's because they gave up zero good NHL players for four-and-a-half reasonably priced years of a guy who should serve as a really great second-line center on a contender. Montreal is already pretty busy with nifty young forwards, but the 30-year-old Larkin should slot in nicely thanks to his two-way talents and goalscoring pedigree. Playing on by far the most stacked team that's ever employed him, he won't be the focal point that he was in Detroit, but it shouldn't be hard for him to find a place in the hearts of fans who were chanting "We want Larkin!" the last time he visited.So far this season, at 14-6-4, the Canadiens sit comfortably in playoff position but are in no state to refuse more help. Their young superstars, plus the tier below, are producing less than they were when they set a torrid pace last year, while goaltender Jakub Dobes, coming off a strong rookie campaign, now backs up the even-younger Jacob Fowler. I'm looking at the 22-year-old winger Juraj Slafkovsky (two goals, after 30 last year) as the guy who stands to benefit most from having Larkin as his center. But his arrival should be appreciated by everyone from Cole Caufield and Nick Suzuki on offense to Noah Dobson on defense, because he'll make each individual load a little lighter. Montreal is counting on its core to produce the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 1993, and the current cast will have at minimum four shots at it, with a decent amount of cap space to add even more weapons.

item.title: White House Plots Grand Cover-up of Trump II Corruption and Lawlessness
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: The Mother of All Cover-UpsWith so much to hide, the Trump White House is running scared from oversight by the incoming Democratic Congress, and it shows in the form of performative preemptive resistance that it hopes will run out the clock on the Trump II presidency.It’s a cover-up on a scale never before witnessed in American history, backstopped by a Justice Department under the thumb of the Trump White House that will never prosecute and a Supreme Court that granted wide-ranging presidential immunity.On the heels of the mockable threats to prosecute members of Congress for congressing come two new moves by the White House to interpose itself between Congress and potential witnesses to Trump II wrongdoing. The first was a directive from new Trump Chief of Staff Stephen Miller that federal government employees can’t testify to Congress without pre-approval from the White House.Then on Friday came a new executive order to try to keep government contractors from talking to congressional investigators. Titled “Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting,” the new EO purports to require contractors to notify the White House of “any pending or future congressional request.”Perhaps most importantly, the EO attempts to smother congressional oversight under a blanket of executive privilege. It purports to require government contractors to “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.”As we discussed here last week, government contractors, subcontractors, vendors, and suppliers are a prime target for congressional oversight — a way around the White House’s challenges to congressional subpoenas and spurious executive privilege claims. Recognizing that vulnerability, the Trump White House is now trying to cow government contractors into either not cooperating or slow-rolling their cooperation with Congress — or at the very least to coerce them into giving the White House a heads up on congressional inquiries.As Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck observes, the Miller directive and new EO work together to ensure “that nothing reaches Congress until the White House clears it. That isn’t the law, and it has never been executive branch practice during any prior administration. As with so many other things these days, we’re in uncharted territory on the separation of powers arguments.”We’re starting to test the logical extremes of the unitary executive theory and whether executive privilege shields the entire executive branch from routine congressional oversight.A separate “Fact Sheet” issued by the White House positions the EO as protection against “congressional overreach” — which, it needs to be said, hasn’t even happened since the new Congress hasn’t been sworn in yet. It’s couched in terms of protecting “Americans’ confidential information” from “unauthorized disclosure” to “unauthorized third parties,” including “members of Congress.”To give the EO some teeth, it explicitly threatens government contractors, as former U.S. Attorney Joyce Vance notes:[T]he administration puts the full weight of economic blackmail behind its plan for keeping Congress in the dark about what it’s been up to. The punishment for contractors that respond to Congress’ lawful demands without executive branch approval includes termination or cancellation of contracts and blackslisting (called debarment) of contractors so they can no longer do any work with the federal government.While there’s an almost comical level of gamesmanship and trolling in trying to shut down all avenues to congressional oversight, it’s ultimately a quite serious attempt to cover up the sins of the first two years of Trump’s second term, when the GOP Congress abdicated its constitutional oversight responsibilities.Running out the clock is part of the cover-up. Every skirmish — whether directly between Congress and the White House or indirectly between the White House and third party witnesses who work for the government or government contractors — delays the ultimate reckoning for the depredations of the Trump II presidency.Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC), an 11-term incumbent, has lost her re-election bid following a recount. The race in the NC-05 was finally called over the weekend, and Foxx conceded to her Democratic challenger, Chuck Hubbard.By the Numbers: 2026 House Election: The number of House seats Democrats flipped in North Carolina in this election.: How many seats Democrats added in the House: The number of House seats now held by Democrats, with four races still to be decided: The last election in which Democrats won more House seats than they did in this election.“To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our two-year term.”—Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), struggling to get his conference to show up for theThings That Make You Go, Hmmm …Outgoing Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY) and her family sold the D.C. rowhouse where she has lived while in Congress to a mystery buyer in June for $900,000 over the list price, the WaPo reports.The Trump DOJ continues to “investigate” the 2020 presidential election.On Friday, the FBI conducted a two-hours-plus interview of Richard Barron, the former elections director for Fulton County, Georgia, the NYT reports: “In attendance were two F.B.I. agents and two federal prosecutors, including Dan Bishop, a former congressman from North Carolina and Trump loyalist who was appointed in April as the Justice Department’s top election fraud prosecutor, Mr. Barron said.”Barron agreed to the do the interview voluntarily and not under subpoena, he said.In recent days, federal agents have contacted two other Fulton County officials who worked on the 2020 election, according to the NYT: Nadine Williams, who is now the head of the county’s elections division, and Ralph Jones, who was the county’s voter registration chief.: U.S. District Judge April Perry will herself investigate whether the Trump DOJ lied to her about the Broadview 6 prosecution, rejecting a last-minute bid by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward for her to appoint a special master to do the work. In denying Woodward’s motion on Friday, Judge Perry wrote:The Government has known for more than five months that the Court planned to hold a hearing regarding the conduct of the federal prosecutors in this matter, and for more than three months that potentially privileged communications would be at issue during that hearing.Despite this, the Government waited until 6:50 p.m. the night before potentially privileged materials would be tendered to the Court to file its motion. The request is therefore untimely. Moreover, the substance of the motion reflects a basic misapprehension about what a special master does.: In a memo last week, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter urged Trump DOJ employees not to cite American Bar Association materials, according to Bloomberg, which obtained a copy of the memo. “Department reliance on ABA materials risks legitimizing the ABA and its positions,” McCotter wrote.The Nvidia board has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, saying it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Huang’s reinstatement came after President Trump posted Sunday night on social media that he hoped the board would rehire Huang.Treating Canada Like a Punching BagIn a classified memo last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth imposed new restrictions on the U.S.-Canada defense relationship, including limiting social engagements between American and Canadian service members, such as attending conferences or academic events, the WaPo reports.A man carelessly working on his laptop on the DC Metro train revealed a draft plan for executive firings and sweeping changes at the National Museum of American History, ProPublica reports.

item.title: *15 Best Things I Bought In 2026*
item.content:encoded: Hello and welcome to the first round-up of the season! Today, I will be sharing my top 15 things I bought this year.*!*Next week will be the top 15 things readers bought! You’re gonna love it. I wanted to buy all that shit. I will still add a few more selections if you email them to me BY WEDNESDAY *!*But today is about and stuff that I bought. Nothing in this newsletter is sponsored! I wish sponsors were sending me things, but they are not. These are all things I bought with my because I have when in I’m aware that very few of these things are cheap. Do not add up how much all of these things cost. I haven’t done it and I refuse to. It was a bad year, sue me! But let my mistakes be your shopping list. All of these things would be great gifts and it is the gift buying season!My angel granny dog Georgia turns 13 soon. And in her old age, she contracted a bout of pancreatitis, which meant she had to eat rice for every meal for a few weeks. This was fine except my rice cooker was broken, so I bought a new really fancy one and now I’m addicted to it too! I love that it sings a song and keeps the rice warm for days.When Georgia was sick, I also bought her this Molly Mutt dog bed. Should I have purchased this when she already has so many beds? Probably not, but the purchase turned out to be justified because she loves it and clearly prefers it over all of her other beds.Because everything was so bad last winter, we decided to take a short little weekend away at THE STOCKTON INN in New Jersey. I cannot say enough about how nice this hotel was. The hospitality was personal. The tub was ginormous. I keep thinking about the food we ate in the restaurant. Highly recommend for anyone on the east coast looking for a weekend away. It’s pet friendly, also, and they gave Georgia a special ceramic water bowl. I would die for the Stockton Inn.I bought a little stool with a stained glass eggplant in it from Philadelphia artist Mary Tsai. It’s so whimsical and silly and I love it.I put a photo of The Boston General Store Fish Clips in a newsletter earlier this year, and a bunch of you responded saying they were great and I should buy them. SO I DID! And guess what? They are great! I’ve used them to keep chips closed, and papers together, and even as a bookmark in a pinch. Great little stocking stuffer too.I cook a lot of chicken thighs and the Thermapen thermometer is the best cooking thermometer I’ve ever used. Great purchase. It’s also large which makes it harder for me to lose.My friends Liz & Ashley & Mary and I took a few classes at Butcher’s Sewing Shop in Philadelphia this year. I learned to use the machine, and make a quilt, and make a dress. I don’t really have the attention to detail that sewing rewards, but I loved learning and making shit!I know this is a baby and basic sewist take, but I bought the Singer Heavy Duty as my sewing machine and I’m in love with her!! Plus it’s on sale for Black Friday. If you want to learn to sew, this is a great starter machine (she says, as a beginner)Speaking of learning! I bought myself Spanish classes again this year. Truly, learning a language as an adult is one of the hardest but most fulfilling things I’ve ever done. I first started taking lessons on iTalki, which would be a good gift-card for someone.I finally upgraded from garbage toothbrushes they give me at the dentist to the most basic level Sonicare, and everyone was right: my teeth feel cleaner.While I was in Mexico, I bought these little green mezcal sipping cups at A Mesa Puesto. They’re so cute and I love the way they feel in my handsFriend of the newsletter (me) and brilliant esthetician (book her for facials) Jolie de Feis, gave me the Crown Affair Dry Shampoo powder for my birthday. Unfortunately, this whips. My hair looks better with it in than it does after I wash it, and the little brush applies it evenly so there’s no white cast. I love it because I hate showering.As a big purchase this year, I bought an original painting from Philadelphia artist Ariel Posh. I cannot wait to hang it in my home, and I smile just thinking about it. More than anything, in this terrible stupid AI world, I recommend purchasing real work from real artists you love.As a Christmas present, I bought my partner this Saint Davis custom sapphire (my birthstone!) signet ring. When it showed up in September, I was so excited that I gave it immediately. Whoops! Now I’ll have to buy something else. All of this guy’s designs are really gorgeous and he was a pleasure to work with.Thank you so much for subscribing to this silly newsletter! If you bought something great this year, send it to me by Wednesday! If you are sad there is nothing to read this week, consider Defector.com. I cried reading two articles last week, but you’ll have to guess which ones.

item.title: “I’m not going to remove the repository”
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: There is a hacking tool called ARTEX that is causing havoc around the world. It lets a hacker plug in their LLM of choice, and ARTEX will then spin up a bunch of AI subagents focused on different aspects of hacking, such as scoping out a target or stealing data. This tool can complete an entire hack of a target in just a few hours. The original author of ARTEX took down the tool in October after it became clear that bad people were using it. But, as I write below, ARTEX is free. Several people are still distributing it on GitHub. I spoke to them about it, asked them why, and for their thoughts about requests to take the tool down. And as I’m writing this, NVIDIA just said it has reinstated Jensen Huang as President, CEO, and Board Director. Hahahahahahahahahha.ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage, and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted, hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says, “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere.“I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.”Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue…I had a great chat with Raphael Satter of Reuters about OpenAI’s own out of control hacking. Satter and his colleagues led the coverage on all of that, and Satter ran me through it. I loved the analogies he used, especially about security through obscurity. Oh, no one will try this door, surely? Well, with AI, a hacker can try every door, no matter how obscure. Watch the conversation on YouTube below, or find it in our audio feeds here.a sketchy company claimed it could recover ransomware victims’ data through complex decryption techniques. Really, the company was just paying the hackers and charging the victim. To catch the company in the act, the FBI pretended to be a ransomware victim and hired the firm. Then, to catch the company paying the hackers, the FBI went undercover as this fictitious ransomware gang.Oh, would you look at that. A study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University found that developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods.Jason found that AptDeco, a website for people to sell high-end furniture, wasn’t actually giving people their money. You might have seen the original story, but we have an update. AptDeco blamed AI agent swarms, or something? Jason then told AptDeco, you’re going to need to elaborate if I’m going to update my article with this bizarre statement. AptDeco then admitted, “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.” The company clarified it rolled out improved “protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing.” AptDeco now says that payouts are back, following our coverage.On Monday morning, NVIDIA announced that, effective immediately, “Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board.” You can read the announcement here.“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board, said in that announcement. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.”Huang, obviously, seems pretty chuffed. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” he said.“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added. I want to point to some of the amazing followup reporting about the whole saga, which uncovered more details of what Alice Huang’s family and companies were actually doing, including getting Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors. But I guess that’s all good, don’t worry about it. We’re back, baby.In you communicate with your criminal conspirators through a clear knockoff of WhatsApp. It even says “messages encrypted” at the top. Pavel Durov, CEO of Telegram, has thoughts: “The least realistic thing about GTA VI is that Jason and Lucia run a whole criminal operation without a single Telegram group,” on Sunday. He admit it! Telegram is an app heavily used by criminals! Even if they probably shouldn’t, because Telegram’s end-to-end encryption isn’t on by default. I guess the game’s protagonists do prefer encryption by default. Signal is making a big change where the ability to take screenshots of the app is going to be off by default. Why? Because of AI, of course. As mobile operating systems (and Windows) introduce more AI, Signal doesn’t want chats getting read by AI agents. “In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents ‘scan’ the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding,” Signal’s announcement reads.That’s the newsletter for today. They did mention VPNs in GTA 6.

item.title: Let’s all watch a Donny impersonator in Canada mock the shit out of Preznit Fuckwit
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Let’s start today’s post with a bang, and put our Hero of the Day right up top.Saturday night, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke at the annual Parliamentary Press Gallery Dinner in Ottawa — and he brought a ringer with him: comedian Mark Critch, who spent three awesome minutes mocking the shit out of Donny Convict.“He’s got a great ass, doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass. He’s got such an incredible ass.”Critch nailed it. He had the inane ‘jacking off two invisible giraffes’ dance down pat.He did the infantile handshake, too.And he had Donny’s moronic growly vocal cadences down, as well as his ability to speak in circles while saying absolutely nothing.“And we’re going to have a deal, though. We’re gonna have a dear, aren’t we? Mark, we’re going to have an incredible deal. I call him— Mark. I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward. But we’re going to have— A GREAT DEAL. There’s only one thing standing in the way. Me. Because I’m crazy. But that’s okay.”“Damn. This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”Oh look, Canada is openly mocking us now. Canada — the most polite country on the planet.Apparently, as far as I can tell, Canada hasn’t been nuked yet. So I guess that the diaper nurse has somehow kept Dear Leader from seeing these clips.Congratulations are in order to Donny — he’s an international laughingstock. Donny never shuts the fuck up about how much everyone respects him, when the reality is that nothing could be further from the truth. He’s an easily-parodied sideshow clown who prances about in ill-fitting clothes, with that ridiculous rat’s nest of what the fuck even is that stapled to his big, dumb pumpkin head, along with his rotting hands, bloated cankles, and whatever the hell is creating that bulge in his ass. And let’s never forget that voluptuous neckgina.So no, no one in the world is Dear Leader. And no one is his , either. Not Putin, and certainly not Xi. This is basically the world’s reaction to Donny, the second his back is turned:Ace job, Donny — .Face the Nation host Margaret Brennan: “So there were thousands of customers across America, who, when they went to some of the biggest banks, had issues this past week, with tech outages. And it caused a bit of a panic, with people pulling out cash. In this age of AI, what should Americans prepare for, and should they worry about their financial institutions?” Soybean Scott: “No, they shouldn’t. What we are seeing, as they, because of the SI, as they go into a— patch their security systems, the patches may cause a glitch. which is what happened last week. I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine. Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.”I’m sorry, what? What the fuck kind of screwball analogy is that? Why even as this smug, haughty bastard even being asked questions about tech? He’s a bean counter. A number cruncher. He doesn’t know shit about software glitches, or what causes them. Bessent’s job is to cheerlead. He’s never going to tell us the truth. He’s not going to say anything like ‘be fucking terrified, none of us have any clue what’s going on.’I don’t want be told to relax, and that tech outages are actually good for me. I didn’t vote for this shit. None of us did. We didn’t vote for greedy, arrogant tech bros to inflict their fucked-up visions of janky, six-fingered plagiarism robot overlords on us. Can’t they just leave us alone? Can’t they and their personal flotation devices just fuck off to their private islands and never be heard from again?How much fucking money do they need? New kidneys don’t cost much.Now, as we get into this next story, try not to let your head explode. What I’m about to tell you is a big ball of . It seems that Donny’s granny-starving Commerce Secretary, Howard Nutlick, was close to getting fired last year, after it came out that he’d visited Epstein Island.Trump was close to ousting Lutnick earlier this year after Lutnick acknowledged he had visited convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at his private island, according to people familiar with the matter. You’ll never guess how Nutlick saved his job. Actually, you will— goddamn it, sorry, I meant to say . Anyway, you will totally believe how LUT-NICK saved his job, — because it involves corruption.But Lutnick, a billionaire and former chairman of Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald, made a $25 million donation to Trump’s presidential library, and Trump stopped talking about replacing Lutnick, the people said. So Nutlick saved his job by shoveling twenty-five mill— GODDAMMIT, I did it again. Why do I keep doing that?So LUT-NICK kept from being fired by shoveling twenty-five million dollars under the table to his boss. As one does, when one is corrupt as fuck.Remember, Nutlick (fuck it, I’m going to stop correcting myself)— Nutlick is the guy who said that if your granny’s Social Security check fails to show up on time, she should just shut the fuck up about it, because only a scammer would complain about shit like that. “Let’s say Social Security didn’t send out their checks this month. my mother-in-law, who’s 94, wouldn’t call and complain. She wouldn’t call and complain. she just wouldn’t. She’d think something got messed up, and she’ll get it next month. A fraudster always makes the loudest noise, screaming, yelling, and complaining.”I have two words for Howard Nutlick. The first one rhymes with and the second rhymes with This out-of-touch gazillionaire has no idea what it’s like to live on a tight budget. If Granny Nutlick’s check doesn’t show up, she can always phone up Howie and ask him to float her a few large, no biggie.And if Nutlick’s job is on the line because it turns out he’s got his own dead pedo bestie problem, he can just peel twenty-five million off that roll he keeps in his pocket, and hand it off to Dear Leader. As one does, when one is corrupt as fuck.How much is Nutlick personally raking in from his job as Commerce Secretary, if it’s worth A TWENTY FIVE MILLION DOLLAR BRIBE to keep it? That’s the question I want the next Democratic Congress to be asking Nutlick, under oath: ‘how much are you grifting off your job?’What’s really maddening is how the Wall Street Journal normalizes this shit. The gist of their article is basically how awesome Nutlick is at keeping his job. ! The Journal calmly reports on all this as if it ware the most perfectly normal thing in the world — which it is, when Donny and everyone who works for him is corrupt as fuck.Okay, I need to simmer down. I’m just going to watch Piss-Drunk Pete flip a skateboard up into his own nuts, until the vein in my temple stops throbbing.Okay, we’re going to need some Daily Claudia right about now. Look at Ms Spouse and Tenchi the Wonder Cat — , on April 26, 2020.And here’s another pic of Ms Spouse and her bestie Kathy, in the garden of the restaurant Harvest on Hudson on March 13, 2021.Fuck it, let’s do one more pic, from September 6, 2019.Have a great Monday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Trump hasn't changed, and I can prove it
item.author: 1axbqu49uff75phphrh5snssvmfyhlp6soxb6b@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Every time the legacy media declares Donald Trump cured of election denialism, the symptoms flare up again. The latest relapse came over the weekend, when Trump was asked on Fox News about reports that the FBI had been hacked.He found a “positive spin” on the hack. “Maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise,” he said. “… Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place.”Which election did he mean? He didn’t say. With Trump, it hardly matters.In late October, Trump said he would respect the results “if they’re honest elections.” On election night, as Republican losses mounted, he told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept those results.” The legacy media swooned.Yet, six days later, Trump was back to his old lies: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote on Truth Social. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”This weekend Trump was at it again. He called Democrats’ recent electoral sweep a “rather strange ‘win.’”

Trump.

item.title: ‘The Code Is Already Copied Everywhere’: The AI Hacking Tool Causing Havoc Around the World
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage, and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted, hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says, “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere.“I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.”Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue (#61) saying their service had been attacked by someone using ARTEX, and asked that the project be taken down or restricted until safeguards were added,” he told 404 Media in an email. “I replied that the project would stay up, pointing to its authorized-use terms, and suggested they work with law enforcement, which they said they had already contacted.”Tools being available openly is, of course, the nature of open source software, and specifically penetration testing and cybersecurity tools. For decades, cybersecurity defenders have used offensive open source tools to test their own defenses or those of their clients. This lets them simulate what a hacker might do, and they can patch their systems, hopefully, before a hack. But, these tools can also be used by real attackers. Look at Russian state-sponsored hackers using the age old Metasploit framework.What has changed is the “speed and the skill level required” to hack, Jung said. “Agentic tooling compresses steps that used to take a skilled operator days into hours. That is why I think defenders need to understand these tools and have detection signatures for them.”Racem acknowledged the damage that ARTEX is causing. “The harm the [FBI] advisory describes is real, and I don’t minimize it,” they said. “The behaviour it lists (entering systems without authorization, taking data) is a crime, whoever commits it. I’m not going to pretend the tool is harmless: it automates a large part of the manual work of a penetration test, which is why it is useful, and why some people will misuse it. The authorization belongs to the operator, not to the tool.”The reason Racem is hosting it is for small teams, they said. “I also maintain it for people testing their own systems: founders and small teams without a pentest budget can run it against their own infrastructure for the price of some API calls. I have seen people do that, and I use it myself on bug bounty programs and for AI security research,” Racem said.Both Racem and Jung said they don’t know if the FBI advisory is talking about their specific versions of ARTEX, and really, they can’t possibly know. But, both admonished malicious use of the tool. “I take it seriously. Using ARTEX against systems without authorization is exactly what the project’s README and legal notice prohibit, and I’d encourage security teams to check their systems against the indicators of compromise the FBI published,” Jung added.Jung said he has since added an email address people can contact if they think ARTEX was used against their systems.

item.title: Brock Purdy Made The Vikings Go Bust
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: The NFL season presents few things as satisfying as a game that promises to answer questions: Is this team really a contender?Is that guy really an MVP candidate? Does that scheme actually work against good teams? These are a few of the questions that swirled around Sunday night's matchup between the Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers, who came into the game as two of the NFC's best teams, but left the Niners' 35-10 victory as something else.Success against the Vikings depends on one's ability to deal with pressure, and not the metaphorical kind. Brian Flores's defense blitzes at a historically high rate, and in the process of becoming the league's most fearsome defense has raised some interesting philosophical questions about NFL schemes. Should teams just blitz on every down? If not, why hasn't any team punished the Vikings for doing essentially that?Every blitz is a bet that the defense will reach and disrupt the quarterback before he has time to find an open receiver in the vacated space, and it's one that Flores has been winning more often than not. Every gambler with that kind of success rate has an edge, and Flores's seems to be his understanding that, in the aggregate, there just aren't enough good quarterbacks and functional offenses in the league to punish his aggressiveness. Think about how much bad quarterback play happens every Sunday, and ask yourself why any defensive coordinator should hesitate to turn up the pressure on offenses that already struggle with the basics.

item.title: Dangerous Self-Experiments That Paid Off
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Our idea of a mad scientist is one who has nefarious aims while conducting experiments, which is convenient for serving as a villain in a story. It's more common in real life that a scientist is trying to advance knowledge and make the world a better place, but some of them can be a little crazy, or at least somewhat reckless. Today we have ethics boards that stop dangerous experiments and make sure we keep subjects informed of risks. What's an ethical scientist to do? In some cases, when an experiment is just too risky to ask someone else to be a subject, the scientist will try it on themself. That takes both confidence and guts. We've seen scientists and engineers try out something new that failed spectacularly, leading to their deaths (early flying machines come to mind). But there are a few cases in which these self-experiments led to great scientific breakthroughs, and sometimes even a Nobel Prize. This TED-Ed lesson brings us several such stories. Oh, and don't try this at home.

item.title: Site Outages and a Slower Holiday Week
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Hey folks. Like the rest of the internet & other tech infrastructure, KDO has seen some outages in the past week or so, amounting to a few hours of downtime. Our time here together isn’t what I would call mission critical — reading the site an hour or two after you’d originally wanted to is not the worst thing in the world — but it’s still a bummer to have the site be unavailable.The reasons for the KDO downtime have been various, but that it occurred around the same time as some of these other outages isn’t, IMO, coincidental. Security researchers and developers armed with LLMs are going bananas finding exploits in a bunch of the software and infrastructure underpinning, well, everything. On the other side of the aisle, sysadmins are scrambling to fix all of these newly found exploits.But of course, poking holes in things is easier & faster than plugging them. LLMs can help with the patching, but it’s asymmetric warfare — being slow & careful with upgrades and patches isn’t a luxury you have when so many things are coming at you on a daily basis. Hopefully the situation won’t get too much worse before it gets better, but in the meantime, I’m thankful for everyone who is trying to keep these systems running. 🙏Second thing: after a few months on the other side of the world, I’m spending some time with my family for Thanksgiving, and so the site will be a bit slower this week and very early next week. I’ve been pushing quite a bit over the past several weeks and it’s nice to take a bit of a break.

item.title: Boomerhuang
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: It came down to a battle between stock values and ethical values. Ethics never stood a chance. Maybe we should have known all along that the two-week Nvidia saga would result in the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO. First, the market really wanted the bleeding to stop. And second, what plot turn could be more representative of this era than a confirmation that grifting through the betrayal of America’s laws, rules, and values would pay off? Considering the circular financing that drives the AI industry, it was predictable that tech leaders would circle the wagons, led by Sheriff Bone Spurs, who has, in an even more predictable move, taken the credit for Huang getting his old gig back. It seemed like there was near-universal support for Huang’s return among our tech overlords, the NPCs (non patriotic characters) who had the most to lose, and thus rode hell bent for leather (jackets) on Jensen’s behalf.+ Don’t get me wrong. My portfolio is as relieved as the next person’s, but what are we trading for the market bounce? Are we stock traders or stock traitors? The question remains pressing since, even as we’re being told Huang is the right man for the job, we’re also learning more about what went down. (Gift Article): U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair. “The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.” (Now we wait for the news on how much Trump invested in Nvidia right before the reinstatement was announced. Between that return and the money he’s gonna make from the Turkeys who bought Thanksgiving pardons, it’s gonna be a hell of a profitable week.)+ During one of his many interviews this morning, Trump explained: “Losing Jensen would’ve been a tremendous— people say, ‘Is it a threat to have him?’ No. It’s a threat to lose him. And Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee they would give him whatever he wanted.” (Nothing convinces me that Huang wasn’t working against American interests quite like the claim that if he hadn’t gotten his job back, he’d be on the next plane to China.)+ From a purely financial point of view, Nvidia has still outed itself as a company too dependent on a single person. Theoretically, that should be a negative signal to the market. And the notion that the industry is this dependent on one dude with questionable ethics and an overly active libido doesn’t build confidence. The concerns we had about the market yesterday are still there today. James Surowiecki explains: “In order for a build-out to be profitable—which is what investors care about—customers outside the industry will need to start spending huge sums on the product. This can take time; it took close to 30 years after the big commercial-rail build-out started for railroads to become sustainably profitable. In the case of AI, the sums necessary to turn a profit are truly huge. A number of recent studies estimate that AI revenues will have to exceed $3.5 trillion a year or more by 2032 just for companies to earn a 10 percent return on all the capital expenditures they’ve made so far.” (Gift Article): Air Is Easing Out of the AI Bubble. (I suppose air easing out beats the bubble popping.)+ Speaking of air easing out, a lot of it was easing out of Trump’s mouth on Monday. Including this interesting statement. “I protected Elon in my first term … you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me. And a certain incident took place, which was a tough incident.”+ You and your loved ones can try to narrow things down as to which of the many possible “tough incidents” Trump might be talking about during your Thanksgiving dinner. Or, I suppose, you can just be thankful your personal net worth is back to a level where you can afford a turkey. From my stock portfolio to yours, have a great Thanksgiving and I’ll see you next week!“Then came COVID. Many blue states had mask mandates, vaccine mandates, and prolonged school closures. Several of them placed new restrictions on policing after George Floyd’s murder or required the teaching of LGBTQ issues in public-school classrooms. Governor Ron DeSantis seized the opportunity to advertise Florida as a warm refuge from the cold winds of wokeness. He offered police officers a financial reward if they moved there from another state. He proclaimed the rise of the ‘free state of Florida’—even adding the line to highway welcome signs.” Olga Khazan with an interesting look at The Big Reason Florida Is Still Red. In short, the state spent years attracting the voters who helped to keep the state red (and the legend of Florida Man intact).“AI, can you be my friend … I feel like I am breathing through a straw a lot of the time. Is this a symptom of anxiety … Is taking 10 aspirin tablets fatal for a 13 year old 90 pound girl … I have had mental problems since 3rd grade, and I only now realize it … Talk to me…I am 13 and need someone to lean on. VERY short responses please.” (Gift Article): What Google’s Classroom AI Sees. “Kids can treat Google’s school AI tools as confidants. A recent lawsuit argues it endangers them.”Let’s focus on a less threatening, though no less heated, conflict with China. Americanized Mahjong. America Loves Mahjong. Chinese Americans Hardly Recognize It. “Critics have accused a few entrepreneurs of profiting from American mahjong, while disrespecting the game’s cultural heritage. Those detractors have focused on boutique tile sets — often priced around $400 and marketed as “modern” and ‘refreshed’ — which swap out the traditional Chinese characters or designs for Western motifs like cowboy boots and palm trees.”+ Have a great Thanksgiving.
