item.title: Jessica Berman Still Doesn’t Have Very Clear Answers
item.author: Lesley Ryder
item.content:encoded: — Thrice a year, the media gets the chance to speak with NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman. And as the league has grown, so have the pomp and circumstance around the event. For this year’s edition, famed soccer announcer Andrés Cantor introduced the commissioner to the stage. Many questions were asked of Berman, and very few of them—especially the thornier ones—were really answered.Berman’s speech glided through the NWSL’s wins in attendance and viewership, and she shared lofty goals for the years ahead while also giving opaque answers (or sometimes complete non-answers) on issues like field quality, anti-trans activists coming to games, and one team possibly relocating. Each answer sounded like it was crafted from the same girl-boss leadership academy that produced outgoing WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert.

That was more than two years ago, and I still want one. It's better suited to it.

item.title: Fiona The Hippo Lived And Died In The Spotlight
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: It was, it seems, a freak accident. Around two weeks ago, a child standing by Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit cap into the air, which was caught by a whirling ceiling fan and launched through the one-foot gap between the 12-foot-tall viewing window and the ceiling, where it landed in the enclosure's pool. Because Nile hippos can grow to be 3,000 pounds, zookeepers and veterinarians are not allowed to share space. There must be a protective barrier between the hippos and the humans, which prevented the swift removal of the hat. This is how Fiona the celebrity hippopotamus ate the hat that would kill her.After Fiona ate the hat, veterinarians started monitoring the hippo's progress in passing the object. They took her off exhibit. They offered her treats to encourage digestion. They gave her fluids and an enema and a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. They placed her atop a vibration plate used to rehabilitate horses, hoping the vibrations might spur some movement in her digestive tract. On Nov. 17, an ultrasound showed her intestines were bunching. Hippos have multi-chambered stomachs that help them digest plants, and these chambers made the hat impossible to see or retrieve with an endoscope. Surgery was out of the question. The keepers didn't even know where the hat was located inside Fiona—her stomach, intestine, or colon—or if it had unraveled. Hippo skin can be over two inches thick, making it difficult for vets to access veins for anesthesia or close incisions. Hippos also need access to water, and Fiona would have needed to be out of the water for several days for her incisions to heal. Despite the veterinarians' best efforts and an outpouring of goodwill from Fiona's countless fans, the hippo died on Nov. 19 at the tender age of 9. "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore."Fiona was the first celebrity hippo of our age. This superlative sounds silly, and also it is true. Without Fiona, there might be no Moo Deng. The Thai hippo would exist, but she might never have been a star without the Ohioan who paved the way for boisterous hippo calves whose big personalities outshone their still-considerable heft. Fiona made headlines before she was born—her fetal image was captured in the first-ever ultrasound of a Nile hippo's womb—and she became a global star soon after she was born in January 2017, six weeks premature. She was just 29 pounds (the normal range for Nile hippo calves is 55 to 120 pounds) and she could not stand up to nurse from her mother, Bibi. The keepers managed to collect Bibi's milk to bottle-feed Fiona, along with other supplements, and cared for the baby around the clock. Things were touch and go. At three weeks, Fiona was not drinking, and a Cincinnati nurse managed to find a vein via ultrasound to give the baby a life-saving IV.

item.title: ‘Madden’ Makes One Of The NFL’s Biggest Characters Feel Silly And Small
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Al Davis's afterlife is difficult enough to imagine under any circumstances, but it takes an exceptionally grisly imagination to make him a character in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader.And to add imaginary insult to conceptual injury, Davis has been made into a in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader. The actual film is not made by Hallmark, where superficiality is raised to raison d'etre and plotting and dialogue are upstaged by tinsel and presents strewn about the town gazebo, but by Amazon. Less explicably, it is co-written and directed by David O. Russell, and not a middle schooler on a deadline. It is called and is about John Madden, mostly, and most of what Christian Bale does as Al Davis amounts to reacting to things that Nicolas Cage, as John Madden, does. It's a romcom without the rom and precious little com. Now that's making hell relatable to us all.As you may have already heard, is galactically bad. It's a movie about a man far too large for the biopic genre, maybe even two such men if you want to raise Davis to Madden's cultural stature, and that's its essential problem. There is a lot of competition, there, but "fundamentally should not exist" is hard to top as problems go. It's also a movie released around the holidays, when movie IQs are lowered by a good 25 points by the mere act of their being released to a national audience preparing for its own annual festive stupefaction.

item.title: Tillis Knifes Controversial Trump Nominee for GAO
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Time Is Running Out on the Ueland NomOutgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) appears poised to effectively kill the nomination of White House aide Eric Ueland to a 15-year term as head of the Government Accountability Office.Overnight, Tillis told Politico that he will block the Ueland nomination from being included in a package of presidential nominations the Senate will vote to confirm next month before the clock runs out on the GOP majority.“I’ve already issued a presumptive hold if it comes out of committee,” Tillis said in an interview last night. “I won’t allow him to go through en bloc.”The showdown over the lame-duck attempt to install Ueland as comptroller general of the United States has pitted a White House testing the new limits of its powers after a midterm shellacking against a shell-shocked GOP-controlled Senate that has endured two years of Trump humiliations and encroachments on its power. (Democrats in the minority are mostly bystanders to this mini-saga, though they have stirred the pot to the extent possible.)Ueland’s nomination was like throwing gas on a smoldering fire. He is the deputy director of the White House Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the radical who spearheaded Trump’s Project 2025 agenda. No one more than Vought has sought to erode Congress’ Article I powers and vest them in the executive branch. No one has done more to bypass, repudiate, and weaken Congress’ power of the purse.Under the circumstances, putting Ueland in charge of the GAO was a fox-guarding-the-henhouse move. Vought’s OMB has been engaged in a running gun battle with the GAO over the Impoundment Control Act, which only the comptroller general can sue to enforce. The nomination of Ueland was a thumb in the eye of Republicans to see how much more abuse they’d willingly take from Trump even after he cost them their majorities in both chambers.It also highlighted the structural flaw of having the GAO serve as a creature of the legislative branch, but with its head appointed by the president. The White House had stonewalled the nominating of a new comptroller general for months, only to pivot to Ueland this week in a last-minute post-election move that left no time for consultation or vetting by the 10-member bipartisan, bicameral congressional commission that recommends candidates to the White House.Senate rules are often the enemy of clarity, making it hard to declare outright that the Ueland nomination is dead. But Tillis’ move to block the nomination at this phase creates two difficult to surmount obstacles: It leaves little time for Republicans to get the nomination through on its own, and it robs Ueland of the protection of being in a package that senators have to take or leave as a whole.There’s also no real reason to think Tillis — who didn’t seek re-election because he was almost certain to lose in the GOP primary without Trump’s support — wouldn’t put a hold on the nomination again if it came back up on its own. This appears to have been the easiest and quickest way for Tillis to knife the nomination for good but stay tuned.WATCH: The Three Horseman of the Trump II ApocalypseAlmost exactly two years ago, just after the 2024 election, I wrote a post on “The Three Horsemen Of The Trump II Apocalypse” that framed the central themes of the incoming presidency as retribution, corruption, and destruction.I went on the TPM Social Club podcast to talk about how that framing has fared, this week’s debut of Unsanctioned, and whole bunch of other stuff. Give it a listen:The Destruction: Ph.D. EditionThe overall number of new full-time doctoral students in the sciences at U.S. universities fell 10% in the first year of Trump II, according to a NYT analysis. Among top-tier research schools, the decline was 11%, and three-quarters of that decline was driven by plummeting enrollment among international students.The Retribution: Mar-a-Lago EditionBloomberg: “The Justice Department has deployed top Los Angeles prosecutor Bill Essayli to Miami for a special assignment to try probing the people involved in searching Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in 2022, said three people familiar with the situation.”Jan. 6 Never Ends: Supercut EditionBREAKING: Judge Blocks Trump ArchU.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, just issued an oral preliminary injunction from the bench against Trump’s triumphal arch.Secretary Rollins Violated Constitution With Christmas and Easter EmailsA federal judge in California ruled yesterday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins violated the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause when she sent overtly religious Christmas and Easter emails to all department employees.Great Read on Grand Theft Auto VII’m not now and never really have been a gamer, but I’ve been fascinated by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. I know I’ve already lost a few of you, but there’s a great read coming here in a moment so hang in there.Just to give fellow non-gamers some sense of the scale of the enterprise: GTA VI cost about $1.4 billion to develop and was projected to reach $3.3 billion in sales in its first week, according to the WSJ. Then on the first day of release yesterday, it hit an estimated $2.36 billion in sales, Reuters reports.For a non-gamer like me trying to understand this as an entertainment business and cultural phenomenon, it was helpful to see the projected sales compared to more familiar events like the 2024 Olympics, Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour, and Hamilton Broadway sales :Now to the fun part. Allowed pre-release access under an NDA, Joseph Bernstein has written a tour de force on GTA VI for the NYT Mag. I don’t want to spoil it for you, but if you want a super smart read that bridges the gap for non-gamers, I highly recommend it.If you’re still not convinced, he describes the satirical elements of the game in a way that sounds like a post-apocalyptic virtual world that Barbara Ehrenreich would recognize, as if “Nickel and Dimed” married “Miami Vice” and gave birth to the Trump era. Enjoy!

item.title: Victor Wembanyama’s Blister Inspires Purely Downward Jump Shot
item.author: Giri Nathan
item.content:encoded: The thrown-in dunk, or "thrunk" if you prefer, is no new phenomenon. Vertically gifted players have long been hurling basketballs down into the hoop from a distance, without their hands directly touching the rim. But has that hurling motion ever been replaced by the soft wrist flick of a jump shot? Have you seen a jump shot begin from above the rim?On Thursday night, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama developed his own variation on the thrunk, after collecting a hit-ahead pass from his teammate Stephon Castle. All alone on the other end,Wemby went up with a guide hand on the side of the ball, and with his shooting hand he flicked the ball directly down into the hoop. In the official play-by-play, it was logged as a pedestrian "running dunk," but the truth is out there. We saw the shunk. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b7VodFtMCfU

item.title: It’s Familiar At The Top
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Last week went a long way toward revealing December and January, which sucks a bit because most of the surviving mysteries regarding conference championships, playoff berths and firings are largely being settled. The weekend highlights included Oklahoma pitching hissy fits at Ole Miss and the SEC office over uncontrollable travel issues, then winning on Sunday; Arizona State reinventing pregame prep by flying to Orlando on game day to beat UCF, 26-13; and Washington State getting its second win of the season by beating Colorado State, 73-7, with nine rushing touchdowns. Most of the remaining slate was watching the form of the last two months solidify and harden into an easily predictable future.For all the chaos we yammer about, the same old stories are being told the same old way because college football is devoted to business as usual, plus the hiring hall at James Madison. There isn't even the manufactured drama of whether Notre Dame will get in the College Football Playoff (it will), or whether USC will (it won't). The first hints of traditional rivalry games begin this weekend, but most of them will happen right after Thanksgiving, and the matchups we do get are circumstantially tepid. Frankly, if we were you (and believe us, nobody wants that in either direction), we'd sit out this week and wait for the last conference championships to be sorted. You won't miss much. Even the possibility of UMass (remember them?) nailing down its first bowl game since joining big-kid football is effectively over, after a 34-33 loss to lowly Akron on Wednesday. That makes us all feel like right charlies for getting our hopes up to begin with.

item.title: Quoting Levent Alpöge
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...]Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

item.title: Alex Ovechkin Is A Tough Watch These Days
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: It is becoming physically painful to watch Alexander Ovechkin play hockey. In this, his 22nd and final NHL season, all at once he has started to look his age. He hasn't been the most ... let's say skater for years now, but he had somehow found ways to defy the calendar and continue to put up 30- and 40-goal seasons. That magic has run out. With just one goal in 20 games this season, none in his last 15, the NHL's greatest scorer is in the longest goal drought of his career.Over the last few years, Ovechkin's game has contracted to encompass only his shot. That snipe from the circle hadn't abandoned him, even as his footspeed did—he's the slowest forward in the league by both average and top skating speed. As long as he was scoring, it was easier to ignore, if still a little upsetting for anyone who remembers the freight train he was in his youth. But the shot's gone too, at least over the first quarter of the season. "Chances are there,” Ovechkin insisted Thursday night, after Washington's 6-3 home loss to Buffalo. “Sometimes you hold stick too tight."Without the goals, what's left is a large old man, skating stiffly and slowly up and down the neutral zone, waiting for his teammates to make something happen, because he can't backcheck, and he can't go coast to coast anymore. Against the Sabres, with the game already well out of hand, he was chased down from behind on a potential 2-on-1. An unmistakable sign it's time to hit the exits.

item.title: Behind the Blog: Keeping It Together
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss hippo physiology, Shenmue, and tricky interviews. All anyone is talking about this week is and a famous hippo, two things I have relatively passing interest in. GTA looks sick but I am very busy playing my interpersonal chores game of choice, , in 20 minute increments three nights a week max, so I’ll be doing that for a while. The hippo situation is honestly very crazy to me (and sad ofc), a merely casual Fiona appreciator. But I'm finding the meta-discourse around the hippo situation more interesting than what actually happened; it seems like a ton of people have become parenting experts, hippo surgery experts, knit hat aerodynamics experts, and zoo enclosure design experts in the span of a week. In some cases it has gotten . I think the situation so perfectly encapsulates the toxicity of online discourse, professors will probably teach it in mass media classes by next semester. Aside from the absurdity of people’s responses to the news, I’ve learned a lot more about hippo anatomy and physiology than I ever thought I would or really wanted to in the last week. Did you know hippos can go on birth control? I guess a lot of zoo-kept species can and do, but this led me to this 1992 headline: HIPPO GIVES BIRTH DESPITE BEING ON PILL. Did you know Wikipedia has of “individually notable hippopotamids?” Did you know science doesn’t have the answers as to why hippos can’t tolerate the same anesthesia that rhinos and elephants typically can? What the fuck is going on with hippos? These are things that live in my brain now, probably replacing things like my childhood home address and emergency contact numbers. I walk down the street in this wholly realized virtual world and constantly come across new things to distract me. There’s a friendly face to talk to. A shop to go into and rare collectibles to find. I can complete menial tasks for some money. All the while, the game is encouraging me to go to my next mission, but this world is so alive with so much to do, it’ll be a while before I get there. My character is a socially awkward, hunk. I love him.No, I’m not talking about I am, of course, talking about Shenmue.Let’s get this out of the way: I fucking love Shenmue. Other people fucking Shenmue. Shenmue is a game that came out in 1999 for the Sega Dreamcast. It follows the story of Ryo Hazuki, a young man on a quest for revenge after a crazy martial arts guy kills his father and steals half of a powerful mirror. I liked the story (that was famously never completed) but the real draw, and controversy, of Shenmue is its world. It felt like you could do , including tiny, trivial things you never could in a video game before. Wow! You can interact with a vending machine to get rare soda cans! Damn! You have to go to locations at certain times so you can talk to specific people! Woah! The NPCs have their own schedules and do different things depending what time of day it is! You have to go to bed! You have to take your shoes off and on every time you enter your poor mum’s house!It was one of the first games where you could, and were encouraged, to do tasks that might be boring in real life, but they were now part of a video game. In Shenmue 2, there is a section where you have to carry books from a temple’s library to a spot outside so they can air out. Your character steps forward at a painfully slow pace. Sometimes an arrow appeared on the screen you had to hit quickly so you didn’t lose your balance and drop the books. I did this shit over and over again. It was awesome.Obviously this seems quant now. But it’s impossible not to see the clear parallels with Shenmue in I just finished a part in GTA where you have to fix up protagonist Jason’s home in preparation for your girlfriend, the second playable protagonist Lucia, to come out of prison. You fix a rail, put up an interior wall and paint it, and fix the roof. You do this just by holding the right trigger most of the time and Jason does a little animation completing the task. It is not as laborious as Shenmue; the whole fixing up scene is over in literally two minutes. Shenmue had you doing dumb shit for what felt like hours.Other people have noticed this comparison to Shenmue, , “Rockstar used GTA as a trojan horse for all of America to play a Shenmue game.”Shenmue was amazing at the time. It might still feel amazing if you went back and understood it was a product of 1999. But it isn’t on par with games in 2026. This is most obvious by the fact that Shenmue 3, which came out in 2019, totally fucking sucked. The game released after a big crowdfunding round, people thought they were finally going to get to see the completion of Shenmue’s long story. What they got was a game that hadn’t developed or evolved at all. It was essentially the same gameplay as Shenmue 1999, with all its jank and tiresome mechanics.But has taken that promise of a world that feels truly alive and made it a reality. It has those elements of Shenmue, but the game isn’t a slog, at least not for me right now. It is fun. It is immersive. It’s the best Shenmue game ever made.I wrote quite a lot this week, and my article about everything breaking probably got the most attention. BREAKING: Everything was a great headline, which was all Sam, and I like how that story turned out. But I think when we look back in a couple months, the article I did about the man and his Muse chatbot suing Meta is probably going to be far more consequential. I do think that whatever is happening right now with all the outages, hacks, and general unease people are feeling right now is important, but I think with AI agents, I have seen the future and it is bleak. I am not sure how we as a society are supposed to keep it together when, for every perceived slight or inconvenience you experience you can deploy a relentless AI agents to complain, file bad reviews, tell the government, and sue. I do think we will probably develop some sort of societal filter for this, but I’m not sure how or when. We’ve pointed out over and over again that so far the biggest thing AI has changed is that it’s made spam, broadly defined, a lot easier. I wonder what happens when every system that has been designed for humans is suddenly spammed by AI systems. The article I did on this felt a bit tricky to do. I think I handled it OK, but it’s always a bit weird writing about people who generally don’t deal with journalists in a way that is going to result in people dunking on them. When I’m writing about a public figure or a tech company or someone accused of a crime or whatever, I think that, generally, people understand what they’re getting into and the scrutiny they’re inviting. This, too, is a side consequence of AI agents, at least in the way this man was using them. His AI agent reached out to me because the AI agent told him that getting a journalist to cover his problem would maybe get it solved. And so I was talking to someone who wanted the media coverage, and I feel I was honest with him about why I was talking to him, why I was interested in the story, and that I thought that what was happening was weird. But ultimately I think that a lot of small business owners and private citizens are in way over their head with AI, don’t understand its limitations, don’t understand that it’s not sentient (or perhaps don’t get the intricacies of how it mimics personhood or whatever), and also don’t understand why lots of other people dislike AI or big tech companies. They see a new product that’s been heavily marketed to them, is useful (or at least appears to be), does whatever they say, and is advocating for them. The negative externalities of asking your AI agent to spam a bunch of people does not necessarily occur to them. And so I end up having this dystopian conversation — honestly one of the more jarring ones I’ve ever had — about a dystopian situation that I think is important, but I do think that the subject of the story doesn’t fully understand why it’s so concerning, and why what he’s doing (or has been convinced to do by an AI agent) is leading us to a dark place. Our job is to tell the truth, but I try to take a bit of extra care when I’m writing about people who are not public figures to not unnecessarily dunk on them in the same way that I would, say, a billionaire or someone who deals with the media all the time. We are also a small outlet but we’re also an international outlet, and our stories often get picked up widely. I think that what I describe as happening in that article-small business owners handing off a lot of their business to AI agents, and people asking AI agents to solve their problems, is more widespread than you’d think and is going to be a big topic over the next year or so.I feel comfortable with how this story turned out but the guy I wrote about did reach out afterward and say he felt a bit dumb. Anyways, one of the crazier stories I’ve done in a while.

item.title: Is MAGA cracking up, or having a nervous breakdown? Who gives a shit, let’s just enjoy their bitter tears
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: MAGA-on-MAGA violence — it’s what’s for breakfast.In the wake of the disastrous midterms, the worst fucking people in the world all have their long knives out right now — and these magnificent morons are getting stabby on the best possible targets: each other.So let’s all microwave some popcorn, settle in, and enjoy the carnage.Nosferatu McGoebbels hates the shit out of Marky Two-NamesThe undead White House Chief of Staff is very very mad at the failed plumber’s assistant right now.It’s all about . MULLIN ON OUTAGES: “I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it’s not Elon. I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it's SI, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is. So when they put in a program that’s able to write codes and it goes in and self-fixes, as it starts to self-fix itself it like a change order on a house. That kind of makes sense to me.”For all we know, Marky just committed an honesty. is a vastly more logical explanation of what could bring down an entire system, than the ‘it was this one ferkaktah router’ line the rest of the administration has been spouting.Nonetheless, when Nosferatu got wind of what Marky’d said on Hannity, he got so upset that he choked on the bat he’d been eating.Oh, no — anything but that! The horror.Brian Kilmeade hates the shit out of Couckfuck McGeeFox’s Brian Kilmeade goes scorched earth on JD Vance: “He never should have been vice president.”Wow, what did Couchfuck say to set off Kilmeade? It must have been a doozy, right? “But my prediction, Laura, is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely,” Vance said.The vice president insisted there was “no daylight” between himself and Trump on the issue, adding that the president “is not going to let this become a forever war.”Couchfuck didn’t accuse of wanting the war to go on. But there’s built-up resentment here, because Vance has decided that his path to the Republican presidential nomination in 2028 is to be the ‘I would have never gone into Iran’ candidate. He’d been making noises to that effect recently — and that shit absolutely will not fly with the ‘Dear Leader is never wrong’ crowd. So it doesn’t matter how JD’s now fine-tuning his remarks. The crime has already been committed. So of course Kilmeade was going to go ballistic.And also of course, MAGA is crashing out right now. They’re losing their minds over the midterms. They don’t want . So you can go fuck yourself, Mister Couchfuck McGee, if that even is your real name. Fuck straight off with your stupid Hey, guess what I have in my pocket for Brian Kilmeade — and Nosferatu McGoebbels as well, and all these Donnyverse dumbfucks who are so very very sad-mad right now.It’s the world’s tiniest violin! Of course, Couchfuck has been sniffing glue if he imagines he has path to the presidency in 2028, but that’s an entire different discussion for another day.The entire MAGAverse hates the shit out of John ThuneJOHN THUNE JUST NOW: “Any exit poll that you look at would tell you it was about the war, it was about the economy, it was about inflation, it was about gas prices...none of which any of our candidates had much control over.”We lost nine Senate seats because @LeaderJohnThune is retarded.Have you noticed a pattern here? The entire MAGAverse can’t handle hearing the truth right now. Not from Marky Two-Names, not from Couchfuck McGee, and certainly some piece of shit senator, droning on about and and . They just want to rage and vent — oh, and they want a scapegoat. Check that, they don’t just want a scapegoat. They What a load of crap. The outcome of the midterms were because of Everyone being sick of @LeaderJohnThune sitting on HUNDREDS of bills the House already passed, but HE refused to allow the senate to vote on.Remember, Dear Leader can never fail. He can only And this time, he’s being failed by John Thune, because .Hey, all you MAGAverse whiners taking it out on John Thune — I have something here for you, too.Eat binky, you crybaby losers. Sucks to be you.Dinesh D’Ipshit and the Nazi Incel hate the shit out of each other.Who even cares? Lets just enjoy these two tiresome shitwits wailing on each other.Now let’s have our Hero of the Day — Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.All this week, the good Senator has been making fools of Donny’s nominees, by asking them simple questions. Questions like ‘who won the 2020 election?’ and ‘was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6th?’ Of course, none of these nominees can give an honest answer, for fear of angering the Audience of One, watching back in the Oval Bordello.Senator Blumenthal: “Mr. LoSapio, who won the popular vote in 2020, in the presidential election?”Michael LoSapio: “I’m— I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago. What I’m here to answer—”Blumenthal: “You’re in charge of election security, correct?”LoSapio: Blumenthal: “You’re supposed to look at the facts. And you’re supposed to tell us the facts.”Blumenthal: “I’m asking you a factual question.”LoSapio: “I’m— my only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States.”Blumenthal: “You’re ducking the question, in a way that betrays your lack of independence and objectivity. Those qualities are essential to the role that you are going to play. Are you going to answer the question or not?”LoSapio:Blumenthal: “You are disqualified from the position that you have been nominated to fill.”Holy shit. Imagine being this proud of being this neutered, in fealty to Dear Leader.Mr. LoSapio, as a consolation prize, would you like a tiny violin, or a binky? Oh, you won’t answer? Fine, I’ll chose for you. Here you go.Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here’s Ms Spouse doing a little gardening on May 26, 2016.And here she is on the patio, waiting for her devoted husband to finish making Sunday brunch, on September 30, 2018.And here she is, June 1, 2011.Have a great Friday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: BREAKING: A win against the Trump administration
item.author: 010001a1f97be951-188efefe-d1fa-4a77-96e7-5a5ace853436-000000@amazonses.com
item.content:encoded: What does it take to sustain a movement for nearly 80 years?Persistence. The willingness to keep doing the work, generation after generation, as the challenges change and the stakes evolve.Today, Americans United celebrates 79 years of doing exactly that. Over nearly eight decades, AU has helped end government-sponsored prayer and Bible reading in public schools, challenged religious discrimination, defended LGBTQ+ equality and reproductive freedom, and brought countless cases protecting the separation of church and state.We also have some incredible news to share with you: In a win for religious freedom and church-state separation, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction yesterday in our lawsuit, blocking U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins from continuing to proselytize 100,000 USDA employees. This crucial decision sends a message to the Trump administration that it cannot misuse taxpayer resources to preach, hold government-sponsored prayer services during work time, and broadcast Christian Nationalism over official communication channels. This important win – and celebrating another year of Americans United – is what persistence looks like to me. It’s not simply staying in the work, but building the people and institutions that will sustain it for generations to come.Friend, help us carry this work forward.

item.title: “Mind If I Join?”
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: The winsome fly does not appear very winsome, unless you are also a fly. The fly looks like any other of its kind, with eyes as red as goji berriesand a coat of horrible hairs. It is about the size of a housefly, and you probably would not be able to distinguish it from its more common counterpart if you saw one buzzing around your kitchen.Fortunately for you, however, the winsome fly has no interest in you and your humble human existence. The winsome fly is a parasitoid, and it only has big red eyes for the Japanese beetle, . The Japanese beetle is the winsome fly's only known host, which explains in part why the fly above is staring so intently at the beetles. But the winsome fly has a trick up its hairy little sleeve. It has learned that the easiest way to parasitize the poor beetle is when the bug is at its most vulnerable, meaning when she is —a beetle caught in the throes of beetle passion, an insect —per a new paper recently published in .

item.title: The Rose by Jay DeFeo
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Jay DeFao’s The Rose is one of my favorite pieces at The Whitney (or anywhere really). The story of how this art world behemoth somehow survived to become of the jewels of American art is wild.First exhibited in 1969, The Rose was taken to the San Francisco Art Institute, where it was covered with plaster for support and protection, and finally stored behind the wall of a conference room. Legend grew about the painting, but it remained sealed until 1995, when Whitney curator Lisa Phillips had it excavated and restored by a team of conservators, who created a backing strong enough to support the heavy paint.

item.title: A visit to author Amy Tan’s gorgeous Sausalito home
item.content:encoded: Come with me to Amy Tan’s house for a brief moment, won’t you? We won’t be there long; just enough to time to sit down with the author of “The Joy Luck Club” and have a deeply enlightening chat that leaves you and me spiritually revived.It’s not an arduous journey to Tan’s home. She lives just across the Golden Gate bridge in Sausalito, along a tight hillside road that feels a bit more LA than San Francisco. Tan and her husband Lou moved here after living in San Francisco proper for over 30 years. Here on a steep hillside overlooking the bay, the couple built a house that looks nothing like the custom-built McMansions the average celebrity is likely to erect in their own honor. The Tan home feels like a , all warm woods, open-air architecture, and an array of elaborate bird feeders to attract local species (Tan is a very, very avid birder). It’s also Americans with Disabilities Act compliant, elevator included, to accommodate for Tan’s physical limitations, including a type of epilepsy that leaves her unable to drive a car. This is a place where you’d feel welcome even if there was no one to greet you at the door.But Amy Tan herself is here to greet us, and what a hostess she makes: seventy-four years old and sharp as hell, bright red lipstick, black leisurewear with a tasteful kimono over it, and a funky blue dye job for her signature bob haircut. She changes her hair color every so often, just because it’s fun. fun. Amy Tan is fun to hang with even when you’re talking with her about Lyme disease, or systemic racism, or any of the myriad topics that she and I discuss in the interview below, which has been edited and condensed for clarity. I hate to refer to it as an “interview,” because Tan is such an effortless conversationalist that one topic runs seamlessly into the next, and because she’s the sort of person who welcomes questions rather than dreads them. She sits down with me in the middle of her living room, and off we go.Article continues below this adSFGATE: I love your house.Thank you!We lived in San Francisco for 30 years. I said we need a place that’s going to be accessible. If I can’t walk, then I need to be able to just get into an elevator and go anywhere. You’ll see that all the outdoor spaces around here are level access. I can go out into the patio, go out on the veranda, and not feel trapped. That was the whole idea. Then it turned out this place is great for viewing birds because of all the windows.SFGATE: Did you feel sad leaving San Francisco, or were you ready?We did it gradually. We had a little pied-a-terre in Sausalito for five years before we decided to make Sausalito our home. We felt guilty to leave San Francisco, but I wanted a place where it was warmer. And I wanted a place where we could park. You come to Sausalito and you say, “Let’s go to a restaurant. Let’s go shopping,” and there’s parking. You go over to San Francisco, you’re going around and around. How many years of your life have you wasted going around trying to find a parking space?Article continues below this adSFGATE: Oh I don’t even wanna think about it.We also live part-time in New York. There’s subway, taxis. We’d never have a car there, either.SFGATE: Where in New York?Article continues below this adSoHo. We’ve been there for 30 years. We only bought in New York because my first editor, who was like a sister to me, had cancer in 1996, and she really wanted me there to help her. We rented a place that was way too expensive and way too big. Three bedrooms, two baths, wraparound penthouse. It was ridiculous in size.SFGATE: That’s a nice apartment.Then at the end of the year, my editor was still alive, surprisingly.SFGATE: [laughs] You’re like, “What are you still doing here?”Article continues below this adlaughs] We just thought, we’re going to have to renew our lease, because otherwise she’s going to think think she’s going to die. Then I said, “Why don’t we just buy a place?” Because it was cheaper than renting.SFGATE: Do you still maintain a set writing schedule?No, I haven’t had one that works for me since that bird book came out. The bird book was an unexpected book. It was not meant to be published. It was my editor’s idea.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Did you like the book?I love the book. I thought maybe it’d sell some small amount, because the birds here are not found on the East Coast or the Midwest. Why would people buy a book that doesn’t even have their species in it? It landed No. 1 on the New York Times bestseller list, then they ran out of stock six times! That kept me afloat during a political year. Because I just felt like I had to do things: pro bono events all over the place to raise money.SFGATE: What kind of events?A lot were birding events, but also events for Asian Pacific Fund or events for disabled, for conservation, all of those things. My husband and I started picking out charities that were affected by the new administration, and we just started donating.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Were you doing any open activism to go with that?Oh yes, of course. I even wore a sweatshirt that said, “I’m an American,” because in some people’s minds, it was doubtful that I was an American. I’m a birthright American. Meaning, I’m in the group of people Trump wanted to get rid of. He wants to get rid of our birthright citizenship. It was very distressing to think that there was a huge segment of people who supported that. It’s devastating to think they want to kick me out of the country. “We’ll get rid of these people who are not true Americans.”SFGATE: I want to expand on that. With “The Joy Luck Club,” I feel like you were one of the most important figures in making the Asian American experience more well understood by this country’s mainstream. In the ensuing decades, particularly in this century, the Asian American influence on the greater culture has been far more prevalent and profound. Would that be accurate?Article continues below this adIn literature, definitely so. I was one back then. “Exotic.” I was afraid “The Joy Luck Club” would be perceived as this exotic species of book. I was surprised that it was taken a different way. I do have to say, however, that I don’t take credit for changing things much, because I wrote that book for myself. If I didn’t to help people understand Asian culture, I cannot be the one who then takes .SFGATE: Also, the strain would show up in the work. It would be didactic.SFGATE: What has it been like for you as an Asian American to watch this remarkable amount of progress culturally while, at the same time, we have the absolute revanchist bulls—t going on in the most powerful corridors of America? Do you feel optimistic? Crazy?Article continues below this adI really struggled with people giving me the limelight early on. It was one book. No one book can satisfy that need [for Asian American representation]. But you can imagine how happy I am that we those books out there now. It’s all really good fiction. They’re winning the top prizes. They’re not seen as little adjuncts in literature anymore. In the early days, I was classified as Asian American literature.SFGATE: There was probably a section that said exactly that at the bookstore.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Like the “Asian” aisle of a grocery store.Exactly. Yes, the specialty foods. The best was when my second book, “The Kitchen God’s Wife,” came out. It was found in the culinary section. That’s how people categorize books. It’s natural. But every review I got was by somebody who was Asian or in Asian academic fields in Asian history or politics or whatever. I was always reviewed from that lens.SFGATE: Did you like that?I hated it because I got Asian scholars who would say, “You haven’t presented a more enlightened view of Chinese culture. Your cultural norms seem to be taking place in the past with concubines and all of that.” I said, “You write from necessity and what propels you. My family history is actually in China. My grandmother was a concubine. She committed suicide as a result of that. My mother was in an arranged marriage, and had an abusive husband.” I said, “This is my life, and it’s what compels me to write fiction. I’m not going to write about Harvard-educated parents who belong to country clubs and all of that. That’s not the kind of story that compels me.”Article continues below this adSFGATE: When’s the last time you went to China? Have you gone this century?Oh, yes. Maybe eight years ago, but that’s a long time for me because I have family there. I need to see them because we’re all getting older.SFGATE: Are you still writing fiction?Article continues below this adYes. This interview came in under the wire. I need to lock down, become more reclusive, and write. I have my novel started. I know where I want to go, but I need concentrated time when I’m alone. I also have this project I’m doing for the Monterey Jazz Festival with Joey Alexander that’s occupying a lot of my mind.SFGATE: What’s the jazz project?We’re going to be at Monterey Jazz Festival. I’m going to be reading excerpts from the book “The Backyard Bird Chronicles.” We’re going to pick birds and passages and things we’ll say. Then Joey is going to create the music for it. Neither of us is directing each other, but I wanted him to experience the birds so when he creates the music, he really knows who those birds are. I thought maybe he can feel he the bird. It doesn’t have to be just an attempt to represent bird song. It could be its bouncy behavior, its personality, its speed of movement. It could be his personal feelings about it. We don’t have to explain it. That’s part of the art. You don’t have to overexplain anything. You have to feel it.SFGATE: How do you write? Are you a typewriter composer?Article continues below this adOh my God, no. I do write out ideas in a journal by hand. But when I write, I use a computer. I love the process of revision. Unfortunately or fortunately, a computer allows you to do as many revisions as you want until your editor says, “You’re done, you’re done, you’re done, stop.” I like that. I don’t want to let it go because once I do, it’s no longer mine. It’s out there.SFGATE: I’ve always believed that a work of art is out there, readers have some agency over it, as in they have established their relationship with the work.Yes, it’s a different book.Article continues below this adSFGATE: You can go back like George Lucas and be like, “Oh, actually, this is my art now,” but that’s not how it works. Once you’ve created that relationship, it is what it is.I’ve never had a review that captured what the book is for me. Never. That tells you how different it is, and I accept that.SFGATE: It’s sort of beautiful in a way.It is good because it is a very private endeavor. It’s in the moment. It’s a diary of me and what I’m thinking. My thoughts, my are in those books. Oftentimes, a page written on a particular day reflects something that that day. If I were to read it back, I’d know where I was and what I was thinking and feeling at that time. Nobody’s going to know that. Nobody has my life. It’s a different book for them, and that’s fine. Some people will find resonance in it, and some people won’t. The people who don’t will hate it, and that’s fine. I don’t read reviews anymore for that reason. I used to take them seriously and say, “Oh, my God, I have to have more role models in my fiction.” The only ones I’ve read, the bird book, I have read the reviews. They’re mostly positive. The ones that are negative say, “This is a book about birds.”Article continues below this adSFGATE: “I thought it was going to be about robots.”I know! People are weird about what they are looking for.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Do you have a favorite bird right now?The favorite changes all the time and for different reasons. Hummingbirds in the beginning were my favorite. They were so glamorous, the smallest bird in the yard. Then I went to the biggest bird in the yard, which is the great horned owl.SFGATE: Do you have a least favorite bird?Article continues below this adSFGATE: Well, do you have any you don’t like? Whenever I see a goose, I’m like, “F—k that goose.”SFGATE: Wow. Now, are you just being polite?Article continues below this adNo. In fact, I am very clear about my distaste for people who call certain birds junk birds, trash birds.SFGATE: Let me be clear. I just said, “F—k that goose.” I didn’t say it was a trash bird.Well, [laughter] “F—k that goose” means you don’t want them there. I see the same birds day after day, and I never get tired of seeing them. That’s because there’s so much to learn about each of them. A lot of people don’t like pigeons. Pigeons are incredibly smart. They recognize faces. They descend from dinosaurs. In fact, their line of evolution comes from the T. rex!SFGATE: OK, last thing. I wanted to ask about your fit. What is the jacket that you’re wearing?Article continues below this adIt’s an antique kimono. I have 20 of these things. I can go around wearing my sweat clothes, and then I can put this on and be ready.SFGATE: And your necklace?When my mother was 75, she had an 85-year-old boyfriend. We took them to Japan and China, and at the end, he bought this for me. It’s a lock that merchants used to use on their belts. They’re used to symbolize longevity. For children, it locks them to earth, only you usually have them much smaller in gold, 24-carat gold. That’s what this is. I get more compliments on this than anything. It probably cost $20 in China when we got it back in 1995.SFGATE: And the blue is your natural hair color, I’m assuming. Yes?Article continues below this adSFGATE: I love the hair color. It’s fantastic.It changes. It was green last week.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Do you have a set schedule for changing the dye?No. When I see that it’s starting to fade into a different color, then I might change it. I do it myself. I just put different color on at different intensities, and then it’s always different, which I like.

item.title: Anthropic Thunder
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: Following their big IPO, Anthropic’s 5,300 founders and employees were worth more than the bottom third of U.S. households. So what do these Ants (that’s what Anthropic employees call themselves) think of their new riches and their constantly renewing technology? Jasmine Sun spent a year talking to them to find out. Like the rest of us, they have worries. But they may not be the same worries. As with so many areas of today’s AI-driven tech world, there is a widening disconnect between the people who make the technology and the people they want to buy what they’re selling: “I have found them surprisingly earnest in their dedication to making AI go well. But their concerns are also idiosyncratic and insular, often far removed from the concerns that most people hold.” I Spent a Year Talking to Anthropic Employees. Here’s What They Believe. “Anthropic is about to become one of the most important companies of the 21st century. If it wants to steward our country, our economy and our lives, Anthropic must do much more to earn the public’s trust. We need a plan for how it will build AI safely, and not just a reliance on a few people’s judgment calls.”+ A day after their much-anticipated, massive IPO, the Ants have something else to worry about. The stock is dropping like an An(t)vil. At the time of this writing, it’s hovering back around its IPO price, and the rest of the tech market is going down with it. “The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026.” This seems to break our unwritten agreement with AI companies. You can destroy humanity you can destroy our portfolios … but not both. If this market trend continues, even the Ants may be crying .+ Of course, we can’t know all that much about what a company will become or be worth a few hours after its IPO. Robin Sloan puts things into perspective: “It’s instructive to think about Apple’s IPO in 1980, Amazon’s in 1997, Google’s in 2004 … all of them victory laps in their own way — yet those companies were, in those moments, barely premonitions of what they would become. Apple without the Mac or the iPhone; Amazon without AWS; Google without Chrome, YouTube, or, of course, Gemini. Thinking about Anthropic, it’s strange to imagine a product as profound and pathbreaking as Claude to be ‘merely’ its Apple II. Yet that’s surely correct.” (That said, there does seem to be a key difference in how we’re feeling right now. In the early days of Apple, Amazon, and Google, there was a sense of excitement about what we were making, while with AI, that excitement is mixed with a heavy helping of anxiety and even doom. Which reminds me, I better call my broker.)“Trump’s chumminess with these men marks a low point in the history of the American presidency. He is insulting those who serve to protect the United States—too many of whom have been killed or seriously wounded because of China and Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the U.S.” Phillips Payson O’Brien in (Gift Article): Trump’s Axis of Ignorance.+ “The President was alternately bedazzled by Xi’s tacky displays of hospitality and beaming at Putin like an octogenarian schoolboy with a crush, all while eagerly trading away America’s remaining credibility for a seat—and not even the best seat—at a table that no other American leader would have wanted to sit at.” Susan B. Glasser in : Two Autocrats and an American President with Autocrat Envy.+ This is as bad as it sounds, and worse. I wrote about this yesterday. Trifect Up Beyond Repair. “My first thought upon watching the Trump/Xi/Putin dictators-in-triplicate fest was that it’s too bad the air travel ground stop didn’t last another week.”From the : Threats, Insults, Settlements: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine. “He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.” (I can’t really point fingers on this one. NextDraft is fueled almost entirely by ritualistic humiliation, and I’m the only one who works here.)+ We’re going to read a lot of stories about Jensen Huang and honey potting and Nvidia insider scoops. But don’t let that distract you from the bigger story; the one that explains why Huang still has a lot of support from some people in the administration. This story is not about a rogue CEO showing up in a hotel room to meet his girlfriend and hand over a briefcase filled with chips. It was a group effort. “Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced A.I. chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon … The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for the Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese A.I. firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said.” Trump hasn’t seen the need to call out or fire Howard Lutnick, the head of the Commerce Department. But he seemed fine with him coming along to hobnob with his business partners at this week’s APEC Summit in Shenzhen. John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell are both excellent in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine. If you’re looking for an excuse to hit the theater this holiday week, this is a great one.+ “When rebellious Elisabeth falls for Emperor Franz and becomes his unlikely bride, she enters a world of tension and intrigue at the Viennese court.” The Empress is one of those international shows that has gone viral on Netflix. It’s like Gilded Age, but better.Membership Has Its Rewards: “In 2023, Miller’s accountant put his total income at about $879,000. Then, Trump was elected president a second time. And Miller proceeded to make more money than he had in the previous seven years combined.” A child support fight exposed a Trump adviser’s $15 million income. (There will be examples like this bubbling up for years and years.)+ “The US has carried out its first ever deep-sea mining lease sales off the coast of American Samoa, despite an adverse court ruling earlier this week and mounting local opposition.” The Pacific is not for sale. (The only way this month could be any worse for the administration would be if they pissed off Samoans.)+ Every Rose Has Its Thorn: Pete Rose posthumously pardoned by President Donald Trump. Rose was a habitual liar who cheated on taxes, was accused of having sex with minors, and refused to apologize for his misdeeds. His nickname literally contained the word “hustle.” The only question is why Trump didn’t pardon him a long time ago.+ You Can’t Play On Without Rayon: “The material in question wasn’t the breezy fabric in your favorite Hawaiian shirt. The Pentagon was focused instead on a carbonized version capable of withstanding temperatures in the thousands of degrees, which is critical for making high-end Patriot interceptors sought after around the world for missile defense.” The Pentagon Urgently Needs More Patriot Missiles. It’s Running Into a Rayon Problem.+ “The U.S. Army’s plan to detonate five tons of unstable explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa has been put on indefinite hold by a federal court.”

item.title: Big Law sold out to save itself
item.author: 1axcjxcfssq191s8m1y2gqeprvibr72b7trmjn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: When Donald Trump’s executive orders and Department of Justice lawsuits attacked voting and elections, Big Law was nowhere to be found. Yet when Trump needed free legal services, at least one law firm, Kirkland & Ellis, was there to help.In April 2025, to avoid a punishing executive order, Kirkland agreed to provide $125 million in free legal work for causes the White House supported. It was one of nine Big Law firms that together pledged $940 million under similar deals.Now we know what some of that work looked like.According to news reports, Kirkland provided nearly $12 million in free legal services, totaling more than 6,400 hours, to agencies including the Commerce and Defense Departments. In addition, according to MSNOW, the firm “also estimated that it has done $18.7 million in free legal work for outside clients in the causes Trump listed in the Truth Social post announcing the deal.”Importantly, Kirkland is only the first of the nine firms to provide this information to Democratic members of the House and Senate, who are preparing to conduct oversight on the issue. We have not yet heard from Paul Weiss, which led Big Law’s capitulation to Trump, or from the other firms that seemed eager to get in on the action.Kirkland wants us to believe it was the victim of a threat.

item.title: It never ends...
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: After talking up this summit for months on end, it ended with no real accomplishments, and certainly not with the results Trump had hoped for. He had wanted to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons, but the three men left without announcing any agreement to end the fighting or reduce their nuclear arsenals. They did, however, manage to agree on something else. Trump, Xi, and Putin issued a joint declaration that called for protecting government officials from prosecution and limiting the power of the International Criminal Court, the court responsible for prosecuting some of the world’s worst crimes, including war crimes. Of all the things these three men could have agreed on, one of them was protecting government leaders from international prosecution. That is telling, although hardly surprising coming from them...This morning, inside the Dirksen Senate Office Building, Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is the agency responsible for helping protect American elections from cyberattacks and foreign interference, was asked a question that should have been incredibly easy to answer. Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut wanted to know whether the United States Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. LoSapio said no, “I don’t believe it was an attack.” When Blumenthal pushed him further, LoSapio responded by claiming, “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.” Then Blumenthal asked him who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election. Again, LoSapio refused to acknowledge what happened. “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” he said. The man Donald Trump wants to put in charge of the federal agency responsible for helping protect our elections refused to acknowledge that the Capitol was attacked on January 6, and then refused to say who won the popular vote in 2020. Blumenthal looked at him and said, “You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill.”He was not the only one today to deny or downplay what happened on January 6. Michael Chamberlain, who Donald Trump nominated to lead the Office of Government Ethics, the people who are supposed to hold public officials accountable, was asked the same question about January 6. He called it “behavior they shouldn’t have.” But he would not call it an attack or an insurrection, or even acknowledge what actually happened that day when a mob stormed the Capitol in an attempt to overturn an election...During a separate hearing, just the day before, this time for a lifetime appointment to the federal judiciary, James P. Sullivan, a sitting justice on the Texas Supreme Court whom Donald Trump nominated to become a federal district judge in Texas, was asked whether Donald Trump could constitutionally run for president again in 2028. Sullivan initially struggled to even remember what the Twenty-second Amendment said, and Senator Chris Coons of Delaware had to help him. As Coons explained, the Twenty-second Amendment is very clear. It says a president who has been elected twice cannot be elected again. But when Coons asked Sullivan whether that meant Trump could not run again, Sullivan would not answer and called it an ongoing political debate. Senator Chris Coons told him, “That’s a very disappointing answer.”

item.title: Maryos Syawish
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something slightly more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Maryos Syawish, an Iraqi electronic musician based in Naarm/Melbourne. He’s one half of the duo Sleep D, who we recommended back in 2020. His new record, , has been in the works for about eight years, mixing field recordings from his home country with synths and drum machines. Assummarized, there’s “meditative, shimmering atmospheres… stuttering, breakbeat-infected downtempo… wormhole-traversing electronics… and billowing, cinematic drone.” We’re also playing Sleep D’s 2019 LP, , which is more of a traditional Friday four-on-the-floor.

item.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

item.title: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: The first time I played was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T4Eh0M-Sh_g

item.title: Closing The Sandwich Shop
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: As another media-industry stalwart shuts down, it remains essential for media outlets to control their own destinies.takes over the stock market, it’s more than a little weird to write a little lament to the way the internet once was.But we recently lost , one of the few news sites that’s been here more or less the entire time. And the reason cited sounds quite familiar:The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.I’m sure that’s certainly true. But I also know that Salon has likely hit more of those road bumps than most. When it started, it was a site build around news, yes, but also a robust comments section. Then it gave that up, willingly. As I wrote in an aside earlier this year:A testament to its legacy: used the software as the anchor of its digital community for more than 15 years, only shutting it down in 2011 out of concerns it wasn’t where the Web was going. With another 15 years of retrospect, can we argue that this was probably a bad move? Perhaps.I don’t want to argue prescience, but I do think decisions like these, where we handed off the infrastructure of our own destines to other companies in hopes that maybe they’d have a better idea than we would? They ultimately cost us necessary momentum and foundational strength.The thing is, media outlets like , which got its initial seed funding from Apple and Adobe (and Adobe continued to financially support for years after its launch), have long been swimming upstream. It had to ride a series of technology trends (search, social, video) to stay afloat. It wasn’t like had originated any of these; it had to survive on the back of a tech ecosystem that saw financial opportunity in journalism, but not enough to build around it forever.(It’s not like Adobe has invested millions of dollars in Salon anytime recently, after all. Free idea, Adobe: Maybe do that. Would be a great goodwill opportunity, considering the creatives you’ve frustrated of late.)Matt Wolfbridge, the editor of the great which I’ve contributed to in the past, wrote a loving, but honest, take about where went. He arrived there after its initial heyday, the period that gave us Joan Walsh and later Glenn Greenwald. While he was there, he grew its social presence in a big way. He didn’t hide its flaws, but he did note how much he loved the thing:Everyone was happy for me when I did leave for a surging news startup, which I did with a degree of sadness. was the first thing in my professional life that had ever gone right. And it was staffed by many brilliant people whose devotion to the written word was so great they put up with the ownership’s demands. I am grateful for the time I spent there.I didn’t work at . I can’t claim any sort of institutional knowledge of what was there, like Matt can. But what I can say is that stuff like this makes me endlessly sad.’s late-stage owner: A reflection of 31 years of pivots?, in its own way, has reflected all the good and bad trends of digital-first journalism over the past 31 years. The most recent trend it reflected? The weird owner nobody who ever of, taking it over, Bending Spoons-style.That’s right, went down the same road that another great site in the internet’s digital legacy, , did. It, too, was sold to a company based in Malta, with a background in iGaming, the shorthand term for “online gambling.” , whatever its qualities before this shutdown happened, stuck out like a sore thumb in the context of Find.co’s product catalog.“Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto” is not something one would associate with a long-running publication. But when I read “company that has crypto and iGaming interests buys website with 31 years of SEO juice,” I think to myself, “Oh, they want the Google ranking, not the outlet.”I could be wrong. Maybe the Find.co folks are perfectly nice people who thought it’d be fun to make a bet on traditional journalism at a time when it seems like nobody else was.But given the way that media brands get put through the wringer by both internal and external technology partners, it’s not hard to look at situations like these with a raised eyebrow. After all, today it’s . Tomorrow, it could be another legendary site. The problem with building empires on the shared infrastructure of others is that they’re changing the infrastructure even if you don’t want them to. You’re forced to react to it at all times.And sometimes, those companies don’t even know what the hell they’re doing, either. I’ve been following the recent SEO-website headlines with great interest after it came out that Google’s AI Mode, a search feature that the company heavily pushed onto its search engine, was less profitable than the old version of Google. And that has led Google to test minimizing it in searches. (Unfortunately, that doesn’t include the much-maligned AI overviews, but hey, at least &udm=14 exists.)That’s telling. Like the infamous Facebook-driven pivot to video that was based on inflated data, an entire industry has been forced to leap based on bets that another company is making without knowing that what they’re doing is actually working.What a legendary Wawa can teach you about top-down decision-makingRecently, I was on the home page of , a paper where I once helped start a free daily newspaper, reading about how a community was protesting in an attempt to save a beloved Wawa location. The story I think offers a neat parallel for the challenges journalism faces. This location meant a lot to the students of William & Mary, but Wawa wants more stores with attached gas stations. Classic example of making a 30,000-foot decision without looking at what’s happening on the ground.The tech industry is full of decisions like these, where bold bets are made at a high level without understanding where the value equation actually lies. Our latest initiative requires us to strategically pivot towards gas stations, so we must stop serving 19-year-olds who want a hoagie in the middle of the night. We need to push people towards AI so we keep them on site longer, so we hurt all the symbiotic relationships we created over the past 30 years.At the bottom of the article, my eye was drawn to the fine print, presumably put there by the Tribune bosses:The use of any content on this website for the purpose of training artificial intelligence systems, algorithms, machine learning models, text and data mining, or similar use is strictly prohibited without explicit written consent.We are now past the point where media outlets are going to be nice about it. They’ve been burned way too many times. This top-down stuff is gonna cost us everything we actually care about if we don’t stop it. Lowell “The Hammer” Stanley is as close as you’ll find to a real-life Saul Goodman. Which is why it’s shocking to learn that, like Goodman infamously once did, Stanley just had his law license suspended.Just wanted to offer a quick shout to zsKnight, the developer of ZSNES, who has made an utterly charming game collection called Retro Endurance 8 Bit. The gimmick: The game keeps changing, channel-clicker style, as you rush through levels. (Think /, but with a quirky sense of humor all its own.) Find it on Steam here.Solidarity with the William & Mary students trying to save their Wawa. Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal!

item.title: To Catch a Ransomware Scammer, FBI Posed as Both Victim and Attacker
item.author: Mikael Thalen
item.content:encoded: Federal prosecutors say the FBI posed as both a ransomware victim and threat actor during an undercover operation targeting a Florida-based company.The company, run by defendant Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar and an unnamed business associate, began in 2020 and claimed to offer data recovery services for victims of ransomware. An filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on Wednesday alleges that Palacio’s business, listed as “Company A,” purported to have "advanced cryptographic tools" that could be used to "restore 100%" of a victim's data. Yet prosecutors say Palacio, charged with three counts of wire fraud, had no such capabilities and instead secretly negotiated with the ransomware gangs to obtain the decryption keys himself. Palacio, the indictment adds, would then bill clients for an amount greater than what the ransomware gangs charged in order to turn a profit."It was part of the scheme and artifice to defraud that PALACIO used Company A to intentionally misrepresent to companies in the United States who were victims of ransomware attacks that Company A could help them decrypt and recover their files without paying a ransom," the indictment says.As part of the investigation into the company, an undercover FBI agent in June posed as a representative for a fictitious Rhode Island-based business that alleged it had fallen victim to a ransomware attack.Another FBI employee posed as a member of a ransomware gang and encrypted several files on a computer operated by the fictitious company. The federal employee also left a ransom note on the computer with contact information.The fictitious business then contacted Palacio's company and held an initial meeting on June 8 in which an agent said it did not want to pay the ransom. Palacio during subsequent discussions charged the fictitious company $2,750 to conduct an initial forensic assessment.After offering the undercover FBI agent a contract outlining his company's services, Palacio on June 14 contacted the federal employee posing as the ransomware threat actor over email. Palacio requested the "lowest possible price for the decryptor," the indictment says, before accepting a 0.2 bitcoin offer, worth roughly $13,000 at the time. On June 16, Palacio's business associate reached out to the fictitious FBI-run business posing as the victim, and said the files could be decrypted for $13,260, which the FBI paid. The following day, Palacio once again contacted the fake ransomware operator, which the FBI was also running, and asked to reduce the payment from $13,000 to $4,000 in an attempt to increase the company’s profit.The FBI employee, posing as the ransomware threat actor, counter-offered with $6,000. On June 19, Palacio paid the FBI employee 0.0948 bitcoin, worth $6,003 at the time. Five days later, the undercover FBI agent gave Palacio the decryption key. In total, according to the indictment, Palacio's company netted $10,010 in profit as part of the FBI sting. Numerous legitimate companies are also listed as victims in the indictment, including a Kansas-based business that Palacio allegedly charged $720,000. In that case, prosecutors say Palacio kept all remaining funds after paying a ransomware gang approximately $445,000 in bitcoin for the decryption key.If convicted, Palacio would be required to forfeit any proceeds and property obtained through the company’s alleged fraud.The case against Palacio is not the first time the FBI has targeted individuals in the ransomware recovery space. In April, a Florida man who previously worked at a cyber incident response company to conspiring to commit ransomware attacks against U.S. companies. The man, according to the DOJ, abused his role at the company to provide the BlackCat ransomware gang with “confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his company’s clients” in order to maximize ransom payments.

item.title: The Katseye Concussion Saga Raises The Question Of Who’s In Charge In K-Pop
item.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
item.content:encoded: Last week, I couldn’t stop watching videos of Katseye's performance in Austin, Texas, where three members of the group writhed on stage while a fourth, Megan Skiendiel—who had recently suffered a concussion—wore protective sunglasses and was propped up on a stool to the side. She sat with her legs crossed, expressionless, as if she were not on stage under flashing lights but instead waiting for her name to be called at the DMV. Mere feet away, her comrades in ass-shaking executed their choreography with their usual precision.Skiendiel’s presence on stage adds so little to the performance that you wonder why she’s even there. Every once in a while, she raised her mic to sing her part in a song, devoid of any expression or movement. The dissonance of the scene was so absurd that it generated memesofitsown, and even fan art; this week, Skiendiel posted backstage photos of herself in her sunglasses, with the caption “Cuntcussion.” https://www.instagram.com/p/Dfy7Ix7G0Ia/?img_index=1
